The controversy as to whether the mummy wheat, so-called because it comes out of the Egyptian mummy cases 3,000 years old, will grow, reminds me of an incident which occurred in Ireland some twenty years since. The rector of a parish there, close To the Curragh Camp, was wont to give addresses rather than sermons at his afternoon ser- vices, so as tc, interest the young officers from the camp. On one memorable Sunday he sermonised upon the mummy pea, ten of which he held in his hand, with photographs of the cultivated pea in flower. He invited all to come to him in the vestry after the service, to see these wonderful germs of the days of Pharaoh. The vestry was cr.y%vded,and everyone handled the ten small peas which were on a silver plate. When the last can bade good-by to the parson there were only three peas left. No doubt the Dther seven are kept in private museums nut that. was the last attempt of the clergyman to illustrate his discourses witn object lessons.

I hear that the later experiments made with the magazine rifle have confirmed the official report that the wearing away of the barrel and the shock to the breech due to the use of cordite can be avoided with comparative ease.

The revenues of the Ecclesiastical Commissioners will be helped by the increased working of coal in Durham this year. The Commissioners take large royalties in that district, and full work (unusual in summer) has been made more general in the county through the strike in Scotland.

The Conservative organisers who would" annex " the Church Defence movement in Wales have had a disappointment. Their desire was that the bishop, deans, and canons who, have promised to take part in the Church Defence gatherings should appear at the meetings arranged by the ordinary Tory associa- tions. This is by no means in accordance with the Church plans, and the invitation—preferred in a hesitating manner—has been refused. Acceptance of it would, it has been pointed out, only serve to alienate the Liberal Churchmen, to whom a partic- ular appeal is to be addressed by these Church dignitaries.

The Independent Labour party are about to in- crease the number of their candidates from 15 to 25. Their movement has been growing at such a prodi- gious rate that all their expectations, .high and sanguine as they were, are completely surpassed. The reports coming in weekly from the provinces all speak of the extraordinary numbers in which working men are joining the organisation. To be- come adherents of the Independent Labour party they must. detach themselves from the Liberal associations, and if the reports which come from the districts are to be relied on, these organisations must be weakened by the secessions. And the men who are flocking to the standard of Mr Keir Hardie and Mr. Tom Mann are not labourers and men of the New Unionism, but tried members of the old unions, who are either fired by the new spirit or disgusted with the old. Liverpool is declared to he one of the centres in which the principles of the new party have won the greatest harvest of recruits. But even granting that all these _reports are over- coloured, there is no doubt about the fact. that the success of the propaganda has been so great that the leaders feel themselves justified in sending an increased number of candidates into the field,

The Oriental is a thin-skinned race. Lately it was the Sultan wno was supposed to be subjected to ridicule in a theatrical burlesque,and the Turkish Ambassador brought the powers of diplomacy into operation to have the obnoxious elements of fun removed. Now it is the character of the Chinese mandarin that is supposed to be exposed to insult in the farcical piece " The Chinaman," which is being performed at the Trafalgar Theatre; and the Chinese Ambassador ti,‘, stirred up the Foreign Office, and the Foreign Office has stirred up the Lord Chamberlain, to direct the attention of Miss Violet Melnotte, the lessee,to the character. In the present case the John Chinaman happens, however, to be an Englishman who has jilted a young lady and disguises himself in the garb of the Chinese to escape from her. The disguise as the piece stood originally was Indian, and not Chinese, and when it was performed in the provinces it was an Indian that the character was represented. Out of defer- ence to the tender f,elings of the Chinese repre- sentatives here it is said that the hero will disguise himself hencefrnth as an Indian again—probably a Parsee, a race not usually supposed to be troubled with thinness of skin.

- , The Tory party in South Paddington, Lord Ran- dolph Churchill's constituency, are manifesting i great differences of opinion on the question of the propriety of putting tim forward as their candidate at the next. election. There are several reasons for . this. Lord Randolph is a collapsed and exhausted force in Parliament, with little prospect ot recover- ing his lost energy and influence. If he is returned, it will only he that he may repeat. some of the piti- ful exhibitions of the last two vears,which were not creditable to the House' his constituency, or him- self. Moreover, his tendency to fly off to other constituencies may be indulged in at an awkward moment for the party—perhaps on the very eve of the election, when a fitting candidate may be diffi- cult to find. The dissatisfaction of the Liberal Unionist section is par icularly strong, and they are , pressing on th-ir Tory frimls the desirability of boldly adopting at once a Liberal Unionist candi- date. But the mass of the Tories would rather re- tain Lord Randolph, with all his defects, than give . their votes to a Liberal Unionist.

Lord Russell is still maintaining the reputation which he has made for himself as vacation judge. His lists have been heavier th.o, tliose with which Mr. Justice Romer had to cope, and yet he has dis- posed of them in even legs timo than that very rapid judge spent over his vacation work. A point of some interest will come before Lord Russell next week as to the right of the Exchange Telegraph Company to cut clf its tape snppli,-4s of information about market prices to a subscriber, in conformity with a resolution passed by the Stock Exchange Committee.

The Custom officials at Themes-street are, I am told, more than surprised to find that two large "runs " of tobacco have been made recently at Hull. That is to say,some tons of tobacco were smuggled, and the Revenue lost a very large sum in the way of duty. The matter was so serious that one of the Commissioners, Mr..Engelbach—the only one,l may say, ler the Chairman is out on leave prepAra- tory to superannuating, and the Deputy Chairman has been transferred to the Mint—went down t Hull to personally investigate the matter. He was quite satisfied that the information received was correct, and he directed a sorv-vor general who knew the place to go dowr to Hull ore day this week, where he met the Liverpool Customs collector and drafted a scheme for the r-organizstion of the star at that port. It is said that a smngoler in prison for plying his trade once too often volun- teered, if the Commissioners of Customs had his sen tence reduced, to make important disclosures. The offer was accepted, and the inforniati.:m sup- plied showed that on these two smu!,glin, opera- tions the Revenue lost between one And two thousand pounds. When it is remembered that at 1,..a1t one hundred officials are employed on the .1-lumber by the Customs to check dlicit traffie, this lack of vigilance is surprising, :mil s,rne important changes in the present system aye likaly to he made.

WELDON's LADIES' JOURNAL.—The newest shape and. latest style in bodices is given as a cut out paper pattert with the October issue of this ever popular magazine. also a choice coloured plate of the very newest designs The number is crowded with novelties in early vrinte. gowns, mantles, cloaks, coats, pretty fashions for chil- dren, smart jackets, skirts, sleeves, collars, dressin,: gowns, evening bodices, and girls' dresses, the direction for Cutting out and making at home are clear and prac- tical. Siere are some very interesting articles on fashions for matrons, how to grow plump, etiquette of weddings, home hints, practical dress, millinery cookery, etc.

Hints for Housewives. The following hints, culled from the " Housewife,' are worth remembering : That rats hate chloride of lime and avoid places where it is exposed. That bathing the face and neck in cold water will often check bleeding at the nose. That wooden and iron ware may be sweetened by scalding with water in which hay has been boiled. That in washing new calico, especially black, if it i• first soaked in salt and water its fading may be pre- vented. That the widespread belief that ivy trained against the walls of a dwelling house,is productive of dampness, is a fallacy. That silver spoons that become discol:alred from con- tact with cooked eggs, may be easily brightened by rubbing with common salt. That a piece of zinc placed on the coals of a hot stove will clean out the stove-pipe. The vapour produced carries off the soot like chemical, decomposition. That lemon juice will whiten' frosting, while cran- berry or strawberry will colour it pink, and the grated rind of an orange,strained through a cloth, will colour it yellow. That a silk dress or cloak put away with dust in the pleats or folds is never so easily cleaned as at fi r- t ; shake the garment well, then rub lightly with a piece ot flannel. That when flies congregate on the upper panes of a window, raise the lower sash a couple of inches, and with a cloth drive the insects down through the space- between the sashes. That warm water will remove dandruff. That grained wood should be washed with cold tea. That cayenne pepper blown int ) the cracks where ants congregate will drive them away. That whole cloves are now used to exterminate moths, Sand are better for that purpose than either tobacco, Cam phor, or cedar shavings. That carpets should be thoroughlF beaten on the wrong side first, and then on the right side ; after which spots may be removed b.; the use of ox-gall or ammonia.

The Ideal. Husband. A series of articles on " The Ideal Husband," to be contributed by various writers, is commenced in the " Young Woman" for October. The first paper written by Lady Jenne, who says that the" real if e husband should be a busy man, and one whose day is very full. Men are not happy without plenty of work ; and a man who has no outlet for his energy elsewhere bestows it on his household, with generally unfavourable results. Small household concerns are not a man's busi- • ness, and nothing is more irritating than the perpetual interference' of a theorist in the small niatters of life. The fin de-siecle daughter of England, speaking of a happy housthold, described it as being one whsre papa and maisima see so Lttle of each other,' and the girl's ji-et was a true observation. In plenty of occupation is the real secret of happiness, but the woman must be content to take the smaller share in the wider and more engross- ing life of the man she lives with. In the wider lives that women now lead it appears as if little of the hard- ships and lot-qualities of which they compla;ned have -vived, and in the general acceptance of that new _ 3itinn by men lies the fundamental reason for the happiness which we believe exists in England in as great a an asure as anywhere. Men have accepted fbi- new role of woman with her greater einancipati.,n, and have shown very little j,alousy of her increasing pfiwer. It may be that the lives of men are in these days more occupied than formally, and that they have net the time or opportunity to curtail the freedom of their 6 better halves ' ; for undoubtedly, on the surface, the imjerhy of men are kind if not ideal husbands,' if w- way judge by the large linerty which married women enj•iy. Many of the unhappy lives we come across are caused by the weaknesses and foolishness of woassn. Tile new life of freedom bestowed on women will, we Iselieve, in time clear some Of the rocks !ind pitfalls out of !he married state. In enlarging the interests and sympathies of women they become much more capable of appreeiatires the wider and broader lines of their husband's career, and more able to be a help and adviser to him.

div.head: DOUBLE LIFE:
div.p: THE DOUBLE LIFE:
Os, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY,
By the Author of " DARKWOOD."
Craprza =ay.

Wt can I pay thee for this noble usage put stplieful praise? So Heaven itself is paid Rows. With the menace of Lord Adlowe ringing in his ears, Geoffrey Trevelyan lifted his unconscious wife and laid her on a sofa. She looked as if dead, and a wild fear possessed him that her soul had indeed fled. He chafed her hands, bathed her face from a carafe of water on the table, and called frantically upon her, by a host of endearing names, to arouse herself for his sake and the sake of their children. His exertions were at length crowned with suc- cess. A faint flush began to colour the marble whiteness of cheek and lip. The chest began to heave gaspingly, and the mouth to tremble. And then consciousness, with its attendant anguish, rolled in one full tide over the soul of the bereaved mother. She started up, and looked around her wildly, crying: "Oh, Geoffrey! he knows all 1 Where is be? Did you call him back? Did you make terms for the restoration of our child ?" . "No, Beatrice ",lsaid her husband, with strange calmness—the calmness of despair. "He is gone His last words were to threaten us all with ruin— you, and me, and our innocent Giralda I" "Oh, Heaven 1" wailed the Lady Beatrice. "Geoffrey, what can we do? I am almost wild? This is a grief bitterer than death ! " "Do not despair utterly, Beatrice, wife " said Geoffrey Trevelyan, rousing himself. "I will set some one on Adlowe's track, and trace him to the presence of our darling. Courage Beatrice—" "Courage, when Adlowe has gOne even now for officers to arrest you I Yes, I have need of courage. Ah, what is that ? " She started abruptly, as she heard a low, per- sistent knocking at the door, and vehement en- treaties to be let in. "It's Meggy " said Trevelyan, starting as if he also heard it for the first time. "She's been knocking this long time, but I had forgotten her, poor creature 1" He went slowly to the door and opened it. The coachman and Meggy were outside, fearfully ex- cited, and both crying. "Come in, Meggy," said her master, quietly. "It's all right, my man. Keep watch of the gate. You had better put up the bar!" The coachman hastened to execute the order, his fears quelled by his master's manner. The keener-eyed Maggie knew that the quiet was that of despair, and went in to her mistress, a prey to the wildest alarm. "Pack up a portmantesu at once, Meggy," said her ladyship. "We must be off before Lord Ad- lowe can return with officers. It's all out, Meggy, —all ! " "Oh, my lady ! " cried Meggy, shocked at hav- ing her suspicions thus confirmed, her voice breaking into sobs. "I tried to keep him out, my lady. Ws fate 1 It's fate ! " "Where are the boys, Meggy ? " asked the Lady Beatrice, looking around. "I sent them out after I saw his face. Send them to me." Meggie hurriei away to do the double bidding. Geoffrey 'Trevelyan walked the floor with hasty steps. The Lady Beatrice wrung her hands silently, her thoughts with her absent daughter. Suddenly a quick, boyish tread sounded in the hall, and then Rupert entered the drawing-room, his face full of curiosity and concern. "Meggy said you wisned to see me, mamma," be said, approaching her. " Ilasa that ,teliow gone whose face at the window scared you so? Was he a robber, or a madman, or drunk, mamma ? " "I cannot answer your questions now, Rupert," replied the Lady Beatrice. "We are all going on a journey immediately. Where is Pay?" "Is he not here ?" asked Rupert, with a won- dering glance around him. "When you sent .us out, mamma, I went upstsirs to papa's study to finish my drawing, and Fay went out into the garden to hunt for his bail which was lost to- day !" "Into the garden I" cried the Lady Beatrice, quick to take alarm. "Run and look for him, Rupert. Cad him!" Rupert sprang out through the open window on his quest. He was absent several minutes, and returned at last unsuccessful, saying that his brother was not to be found on the premises. " Adlowe has carried him off ! " snrieked the un- happy mother, her heart on fire. "On, my child- then ! My poor lost children!" A search was instantly instituted for Fay, the whole household, excepting Muggy, joining in it; but, as before, it was fruitless. The lovely boy had disappeared as completely as if the earth had swallowed him up. "He has either strayed out into the street, hav- ing found the gate open, and will soon return," said the father, his anxiety now almost uncontrol- lable, "or our enemy has seized him as another hostage." He opened the gate and looked up and down the street. No sign of the missing boy was to be seen. No one was in the street at that moment. He called loudly the name of his son, and listened with his whole soul for some response. The only sound that came to his hearing was that caused by a swiftly approaching cab, not yet in sight. With a neavy heart and lagging steps he re- turned to the presence of the Lady Beatrice, who was almost wild. "Have you found him ? " she asked, springing to meet him. "Have you brought me back my boy? Oh, Geoffrey I he is not 'with you! He is lost ! lost ! " "My poor Beatrice!" said Geoffrey Trevelyan, gathering her to his breast. "1 have sent the man over to the station, to see if Fay is there with Adlowe. Be comforted. He will not dare harm the boy." At this moment the bell of the garden gate rang loudly and furiously. "It is Fay returned !" ejaculated Mr. Trevelyan. "It is the officers come to arrest you, Geoffrey !" cried the Lady Beatrice. "All our troubles have come at once. Fate is 'doing its worst now." She sat down in dumb despair, clinging to him as if she meant that death alone should part them. The ringing was heard again, louder and more furious. Meggy came down from the upper rooms, frightened and anxious, her packing finished. Her master sent her to answer the bell, the Lady Beatrice clinging to him wildly, at the same time urging him to fly The two waited a few moments in an eager, ex- pectant attitude, and then as the garden gate clanged shut, a wild hope that their boy had re- turned illumined their souls. "It must be that Fay has returned!" said the Lady Beatrice, in an eager whisper. "Meggy would not admit anyone save a friend." They waited with growing hope. Meggy's step was heard on the porch, and then a quick, springing, manly tread, at sound of which the waiting pair shivered with sudden dread. It was not the step of their missing boy. It must, then, be, they thought, the step of an enemy. Geoffrey Trevelyan—we shall henceforth call him by his true name—placed himself in an atti- tude of self-defence. The Lady Beatrice started up with the wild resolve to shield him with her body. They stood thus when Meggy ushered a stranger into their presence—the young Lord Grosvenor! It was to be seen at a glance that he was no enemy. His noble face invited trust in him. His hazel eyes glowed with friendly feeling, and his snanner was at once gentle and reassuring. He seemed to comprehend at once the state of affairs. "I have the honour of seeing the Lady Beatrice and Senor Arevalo ?" he questioned, bowing to the unhappy couple, who seemed transfixed at sight of him- " Lord Grosvenor I" ejaculated the Lady Bea- trice, recognising him. "You here ?" She looked at him in a wild amazement. "Yes, dear Lady Beatrice, it is I, Paul Gros- venor, your friend," said the young lord, gently. I" Do not distress yourself. --I know all—" "You know all !" interrupted the Lady Bea- trice. 1/4 "I know," said the young lord, with an expres- sion ei testier and levereutial respect, "that you, dear Lady Beatrice, are an honoured wife and mother in secret, while the world believes you single. I know that Senor Arevalo, your husband, is the wronged and maltreated Geoffrey Trevel- yan, upon whose name is a frightful stain, to clear away which I have vowed to devote all my energies." He held out his hand with a winning smile, and Geoffrey Trevelyan took it in his bewilderment, grasping it firmly. _"I fumy also, dear Lads Beatrice." said. the

young visitor, "that Lord Adlowe bas just been here with threats—perhaps with some story con- cerning your daughter—" • "Yes, yes," cried the Lady Beatrice, losing her amazement at this visit in het mother's anguish. "My poor Giralda? a prisoner in his hands 1" "I come here at her request," said the young lord, "to assure you of her safety. I left her this morning under her uncle's roof, in her uncle's care. Lord Adlowe does not yet know of the defeat of his villainous plans." "She is safe! My darling is safe 1" exclaimed the Lady Beatrice, the tears drenching her burning eyes like a hot shower. "You have seen her, Paul 1 She told you about us !" "Yes, Lady Beatrice. Lord Adlowe had carried her to the lonely cottage of his old nurse. It was close to the sea, and only two miles or so from my Welsh piece, the Eagle's Eyrie. I happened to be sailing along the coast. Giralda saw me, and beckoned to me. I had seen her before, and re- cognised her. I rescued her, and restored her to her uncle." "Heaven bless you, Paul ! " murmured the Lady Beatrice, taking his hand. "And then Giralda told you our story?" "She confided all to me, relying on my honour to keep her secret, Lady Beatrice," said the young lord. "The journey was too long for her after her great excitement and fatigue. Dear Lady Beatrice, dear Mr. Trevelyan, I come in Giralda's stead. Let me be to you a younger brother—a—a son !" and he flushed consciously even to his brows. "To clear the stain from Mr. Trevelyan's name shall be my first object and aim in life. Let me help you in this great strait 1" "But why ? " asked Geoffrey Trevelyan, search- ing keenly the handsome sung face. "What has given you this strange interest in one whom even his own uncle believes base and crime-stained? Why do you believe in my innocence? What object have you in my restoration to my rights ? " The young Lord Grosvenor flushed again, more redly than-before. B is eyes flooded with a sudden radiance, and he turned them upon the Lady Beatrice, with an appealing glance. " I—l love Giralda," he said, simply, with a strange humility, as if he were expressing his ad- miration for a star. "And Giralda loves me," he added, with a glad smile and a happy thrill pulsing through his voice, as if he were announcing an incredible fact. " You have known me all my life, dear Lady Beatrice. This is no time to talk to you of my hopes and wishes, but if you will only let me assist you now, I shall know that you don't mean to separate Giralda and me." He spoke eagerly and pleadingly. "This is no time to talk of love," said the Lady Beatrice, beginning to recover from her surprise, and to understand the matter fully. "But, my dear boy," she added, "you shall help us. Heaven knows we need your help. You shall befriend us an Giralda's name, and for Giralda's sake." The face of the young lord glowed with a joyous hope. His eyes were fairly radiant. He lifted her ladyship's hand to his lips, and sought in Mr. Trevelyan's eyes encouragement similar to that accorded so delicately and graciously by the Lady Beatrice. "Yes, my lord," said Giralda's father, with mournful emphasis. "Yes, Paul, we need the as- sistance of a clear head and loving heart. Your face assures us that we can trust you. The Lady Beatrice has accepted your help. Whom she trusts I also trust.' • From that moment Lord Grosvenor loved Geof- frey Trevelyan for himself as well as because of iralda, and believed in his entire innocence of all wrongful intentions, in the past or present, with all the ardour of his young soul. • " The first thing to be dove," said Paul, after he had time to command his emotions, "is to leave The Evergreens at once. Adlowe may re- rn at any moment with policemen to arrest you ! " "We are ready to go," responded Mr. Trevel- yan, his face clouding; "but where are we to go?" " I have thought of that. I have three or four places about the country. In one of them you would be as safe as in a foreign land. I will give you a letter to the person in charge—in fact," he alded, " I have one all ready with me. The Lady Beatrice had better return to town, to watch Ad- luwe nd your interests in that quarter." This plan commended itself by its practicability and common-sense. "But my boy—my Fay 1" exclaimed the Lady Beatrice, recalled to her grief by the sound of Rupert's step in the hall. "Fay ?" questioned the young lord, as Rupert entered the room. "This is our elder son, Rupert," explained Mr. Trevelyan. "Our younger boy was in the garden when Adlowe went away. He has been missing mince. We think that Adlowe carried him off 1" " I know it 1" cried the mother, in anguish. "My boy never grieved sue in his life. He would not do so now by straying away. Oh, no 1 He is a prisoner in Adlowe's hands !" "I think it quite probable," said Lord Grosve- nor, thoughtfully. "But you may rest assured that he will not harm the lad. Ile wants to keep him, that he may make terms with you—perhaps to force you to consent to his marriage with Gixalda ! ' "You do not think," said the Lady Beatrice, in a hollow whisper, "that he means to—to remove him as an obstacle in his succession to the Travel- yan estates? My boys removed—Geoffrey got rid of—Giralda a prisoner, as he thinks his way would be clear ! ' The suggestion struck a chill to Grosvenor's heart. He thought it possible that such thoughts might have occurred to the bold and unscrupulous villain who had so long deemed himself heir of the Trevelyan estates. "Dear Lady Beatrice," he said, reassuredly, "people don't dare form such sweeping schemes of wickedness in these days of law and swift-following punishments. Believe me, Adlowe has taken the boy as a hostage ! Believe me, also, that I will place him in your arms before to-morrow night! But now, let us think of your husband. Although Adlowe may not intend to descend upon hiri at once, he had better depart while he may." "Yes, yes !" faltered the tortured wife and mother. "There may be a spy at the station. Do not go by the train. Have you a carriage?" "Yes, a pony carriage," said Mr. Trevelyan. "Then go in that to some other station on the line. Here is the letter I spoke of, and on it is the address to which you are going. Take Rupert with you, and let the Lady Beatrice remain here until morning. I will escort her ladyship back to town." The young lord turned towards Rupert, and was startled at the anxious look on the lad's face. It was clear that the high spirited boy was puzzled and tortured by the mystery all around him—by his parents' grief, by the loss of his young brother, by the talk of a hurried flight, and the necessity of concealment in some secluded place. "Dear Mr. Trevelyan," said Paul, gently, "make Rupert your confidant to-night. You will find in him an intelligent friend. And now," he added, with a cheerful smile, "I will see if the coachman has not returned, and if the carriage cannot soon be got ready." He went out, leaving the husband and wife and son together to linger over their sad parting. The coachman had not yet returned from the station. Meggy, however, lighted a lantern, and led the young visitor to the stable in the rear of the garden, where he harnessed the pony himself. The task completed, the portmanteau was placed in the carriage, and Lord Grosvenor slowly re- turned toward the dwelling. He had not reached it when the coachman en- tered the garden by means of his pass-key, and the young lord stopped to question him of what he had learned "I've tracked 'em, my lord," said the man, in answer to Grosvenor's inquiries, when Meggy had explained who the visitor was. "Lord Adlowe took the early train to town, and had just left wig% I arrived at the station. He had a fair-haired little lad with him, as he told a guard was his 'fractory son! There wa'nt no time to say anything, as his lordship had barely got his tickets when the train came along. The lad was Master Fay, fast enough, my lord! "Come in, and give your report to the Lady Beatrice and Senor Arevalo," said Grosvenor. The coachman followed the visitor into the dwelling, and communicated his discovery. "My poor boy !" moaned- the Lady Beatrice. "Was he in great distress? Was he frightened?" " I asked the guard, my lady." replied the coach- man, "and he said as how the little fellow doubled UP his fists at his father, as he s'posed Lord Adlowe was, and how he called for help, he thought, but he couldn't be certain on account of the screech of the engine." "My brave boy 1" murmured the mother, be- ginning to recover her courage and strength. "He may attract attention and friends. It will not do to telegraph to have Adlowe stopped. We have too much at stake to hazard anything. My first duty is to MY 1111GbiLlIdi I tnutit n_ot eletaist Ycis

longer, G-eotirey. You must go. I have ttiksrig down the address of your hiding-place, and will let you know all the news concerning Fay." i;eoffrey Trevelyan held his wife close to hit. side, and turned his anguished face towards Gros- venor. "My lord," he said, in a broken voice, "you see how I urn situated. I cannot stir a step to rescue my missing boy. I cannot even linger to console , my poor wife. You have a good face—a feeling. . heart! You love Giralda I By that love, my lord,. I beg you to take the place I should take towards- my loved ones! Do what I would do if I were only free I Find my boy, and restore him to his, mother! Watch over my wife and Giralda. I Do, I ask too much?" "Mr. Trevelyan," responded Lord Grosvenor, solemnly, "I will devote myself to your service. From this moment your interests shall be my own. The Lady Beatrice and her children shall be my desrest, chiefest. care. I will die, if needs be, in. tneir defence. I will know neither peace nor perfect rest until you and yours are happy." He spoke like one making a vow. His eyes, his- facie, his whole being, attested to his stern and un- changeable resolve. He looked to those storm- tossed souls uk. an angel of hope. "We trust you," said Mr. Trevelyan, his tones tremulous. "1 . confide my dear ones to your care." The Lady Beatrice echoed the words. She ha& known the young Lord Grosvenor since his boy. hood, and known him as the soul of chivalrie. honour, truth and generosity. She knew him to be one of those grandly noble souls peculiar to norank sv nation, found among the lofty and the lowly, among savages and civilised people, yet, withal, as rare as black diamonds, or the flowers of the zentury-blossoming aloe. Knowing him, she trusted him. If aught conk"); 'My° assuaged her wifely and motherly anguish in that hour of supreme misery, it was the thought that this gallant young arm Was ready to fight for her loved ones, that this gallant young heart Vat& ready to bleed for her. "And now," she said, when her eyes and her voice had expressed her gratitude to the young lord for his timely aid, " Geofirey, you must go. Take another name—that of Vero. It is simple, and a complete change from Arevalo. Du not trust Rupert out of your sight. And now," she . concluded, " farewell !" div.head: WHEAT AT A HALF PENNY A POUND.
div.p: WHEAT AT A HALF PENNY A POUND.

The average price of wheat has fallen below 203. a quarter. Last week it was only 19 Bd., or less than a halfpenny a pound. Of such a disastrous price it Would (says'the "Standard") be trite to remark, it heats the record in cheapness for, until the present year,it had not been approached nearer than ss. a quarter since a remote period, when money had a very much lindter value than it has now. In a record going back to 1641 no such low price is to be found. Last year's minimum weekly average of 245. Bd. was the lowest up to the , end of that year for over a century. Barley is cheap enough, hut its average last week was 3s. 94. a quarter more than that of wheat, although its weight per quar- ter is 80th. less, and weight for weight, it is of less teed- • ing value. 'The possibility of wheat falling to such a. price would have been laughed to scorn in the days of Cobden. But probably the utmost depth of cheapness has not even yet been reached, as the proportion of damaged new wheat increases week by week, while that of old grain diminishes. Some wheat has been sold at only 143. a quarter in a country market. ,r The question whether wheat-growing pays has now lost all interest. It would riot pay at 204, a quarter in this country if all the land on which it is preduced were rent free, and it does not pay to send wheat here from any part of the world at such a price,unless from a country where there are currency advantagea of quite an exceptional chlrac- ter, such as the enormous premium on gold still exist- ing, though falling, in. the Argentine Republic. Even there it is now declared by an Argentine authority that the price is too low to pay growers at a great distance from the port of shipment, although more than three times the gold price is obtained in a currency which goes nearly as far as ever in payments which the Argen- tine farmer has to make.

div.head: MENTAL STRAIN.
div.p: MENTAL STRAIN.

Every one has a certain amount of nerve power. Call it mental activity, energy. or vitality if you will—it comes to the same thing, and means that each person has a definite capacity for mental work. Curiously, many people do not fully understand that mussular as well as mental work calls for nerve expenditure; that the pedes- trian, the cyclist, or the football player can only call his muscles into persistent and intelligent action by demands upon his nervous system. The individual who possesses - a good store of nervous energy finds his tnu,cles move freely, because his thoughts flow quickly ; as deficiency means indolence, incapacity, and an inferior place in the race of life. In a normal state of health, each person . has, says a medical writer in the "Newcastle Weekly Chronicle," at command, not only a sufficient store of - nerve power to enable him to carry on the ordinary functions of life kthought, motion, respiration,digestion, &c.), but he has beyond this a reserve fund for use on extracrdinary occasions. The misfortune of modern existence has been the discovery of. this store, and the belief that it is unlimited or inexhaustible. Grant that two men have the same amount of mental power. If one works twice as much as the others it follows, other things being (qua!, that one is living twice ! as fast as the other. The moderate worker may attain the age of 80 years; the over-strained may be cut off at 40. The former has lived the " extensive " life, the latter the " inextensive." As society is constituted, we s begin our lives in the wrong way. To begin with, school pressure exerts its baneful influence. Then the father has learned, often, by a bitter experience that profes- sional or commercial life is competition all through, and ;-• he therefore believes he is doing his du y by sending his children to ,chool at an earls- age, and urges upon them , the necessity of taking scholarships and degrees at an . age often all too tender to bear the strain. On the corn- pletion of our education, we are face to face with the necessity of "making a living," but many mistake this, s:s= for a command to become rapidly wealthy or famous, - and so attempt mental efforts beyond their organization. s. We can understand how the literary, artistic., or scientific- s. man may fail to notice where he is drifting to, but it is= difficult to realise the ignorance of the commercial man ; in this matter, why he does not see that, if his object is. ' to accumulate wealth, it should be his first endea,v(ibr to, live long, so as to be able tc guide his investments and give his various schemes time to mature. Many a steady-going business man dies more or less wealthy ; from the simple fact that his life has been prolonged. - "Compound iuterest has enriched his store by the lapse S. of time." We must hope that society is ignorant of the result of , mental strain, rather than it deliberately ignores its con- sequence. Yet these consequences stand out in vivid colours, and should be recognises, by every-one. We cannot escape from the fact that we have a steady in- ‘-r crease of nervous diseases. In 1845, there was but one lunatic in 800; in 1890. one in 341. Then suicide,which is a result of nervous exhaustion, has shown a marked = increase. When will we recognise the fact that the -; greater number of these me'ancholy cases spring from mental strain in the struggle for very existence, or from insa-dinate haste to become wealthy or famous, till at length the exhausted brain gives way to an uncontroll- able craving for rest. What are the signs of mental over-work P They are . the warnings that nature cannot hold out much longer— s exhaustion, irritation, sleeplessness, numbness of the fingers, hand, or foot, dimished power of attention, difis- - in articulation,tvsisting of one corner of the mouth, pain and heat of the head, and all the well-known sighs . of indigestion. Many of these symptcms may be at ,s first ephemeral—come and go—but if the cause be not • removed, the patient may be overtaken by complete s paralysis, epilepsy, softening of the brain, or apoplexy- , With the feeling of exhaustion, irritability, or sleepless- • : ness comes the desire to fly to alcoholic stimulants—the morning nip to recruit the strength during the day, and the glass or two of whisky at night to procure sleep. This is like the needy individual who borrows money lat a high rate of interest. For a time relief is ~ I obtained, but when capital and interest are due. the condition of matters is agoravated. Stimulants can not be converted into healthy mental energy, but food' can ; therefore, careful attention should be given to en- sure a regular supply of light, yet nutritious aliment, ' and not to allow this to be replaced by the ever-at- hand beer,wine, or whiskey. But there is one remedy of the first importance : that is, rest—not more rest and less work,but complete rest. Probably,the consequence of rnental overwork are aggravated by efforts made late --, at night and 'extending into the early morning. It is a . practical idea to sketch the morning as typical of youth, the noon as manli .od,and the evening as old age. and manhood are the ages for work,old age for rest. Let us remember that exercise is the antidote to e%- cessive mental effort. Nature seems to have indicated S this clearly in the modern rush to ambition just at a time when mental activity was perhaps never more pro- s: nounced, and exercise is perhaps the simplest and most effectual promoter of the much to be desired sleep. • We trust our remarks may not ne misunderstood, as the faintest encouragement to mental indolence ; for to be idle is to rust, and duty demands that every mai! , should do his best ; but to endeavour ts work beyosla our powers is neither just to the individual, nor to. society. Moderate, steady, and methodical work will achieve a victory, and bring for us permanent resul: ts • Nay, hard work undertaken as a labour of love will bring its own sweet reward, which will stand out in sharp contrast to the consequences of whipping the brain for the purpose of forcing it to perform work beyond it' 'powers.

div.head: SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.
CORONER'S INQUIRY.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, -held an inquiry on Friday afternoon at the Royal Hotel, Bridge-street. Runcorn, relative to the death of Fred Williams, 31 years of age, blacksmith, recently residing at Dunham-o'th-Hill, who was drowned on the pre- vious Thursday morning by jumping into the Ship Canal, near the Runcorn swing bridge. Thorns Williams, 9, flart'ey-st. said that the de- ceased, who was his brother, had of been very weak and ill. On the previous morning at about six o'clock, be got out of bed and ran away out of the house. Wit- ness suspected that he was not quite right in his mind, and followed him. Be saw him running down Irwell- lane towards the Ship Canal. He shouted for help, and ran as quickly as he could, but he could not catch the deceased when he saw jump into the canal. Some per- sons collected on the bank, and a rope was thrown in the water, hut witness did not see his brother try to grasp it The deceased then sank, and being overcome he (witness) left the place and went home. Edward "'seaman, boatman, of Weston Point, testified that at about twenty minutes past six o'clock on Thurs- day morning he saw the deceased in his shirt sleeves running towa ds the canal and the last witness running after him. Be heard the latter shout for help, and im- mediately afterwards saw the deceased get over the canal wall, on to the rock ground and then jump into the waterway. There was no boat near, and witness ran to a place about 300 yards away and procured a boat-hook and line and returned as quickly as possible to tbe spot where the deceased had entered the water. The latter was on the surface of the wet, r, and witness tried to reach him with the hook, but it was not long enough. He then threw the line to him but deceased made tio attempt to grasp it,although it was well within his reach. Soon afterwards he sank, and was not again • seen alive. By the Coroner : When he saw the deceased and his brother rutining,the latter was some distance behind and could not possibly have stopped him. Be (witness) could swim but not very much, and considered that if he had jumped into the water both of them would have been drowned. He could see that the deceased did not intend to be saved. A lot of people gathered at the spot, many of whom could swim he thought. The Coroner observed that a line might have been tied to someone and that person could have entered the water to save the man. Then, if the rescue could not be effected, the person to whom the line was at-Ached could have been drawn up again out of the water by the people on the bank. The last a itness,in reply to this said he did not think of such an expediment. He could not dive, and could only swim a li•tle. One of the bystanders partially un- dressed htmself,but pa on his clothes again,saying that he could not swim sufficiently to save the man. Guy Preece, lock-master, deposed that when leaving duty at about 6.30 he heard a noise on the opposite side of the canal bank, and could see something in the water. Be was at such a distance, however, that he could not distinguish the object, and thought that it was probab'y a dog in the water,and that the boys were throwing stones at it, as they so often did. He did not hurry, therefore, but walked along at his leisure. Some persons called across to him when he got nearer, and told him a man was in the water. Be at once procured some grappling irons, as the man had then sunk, and he,with other men, began to grapple for the body which they re- covered shortly before ten o'clock. Thomas Williams (recalled) stated that his brother had Said nothing to him of any intention to destroy himself. Witness slept with deceased on the previous night. When be called to his brother, while ruuning after him, the latter made no reply. The Coroner, in a resume of the evidence, said it was a pity that more efforts were not made to save him However, it was easy to think of means—such as that of the attached rope—upon cool reflection after the event but they were not often thought of in the moment of emergency. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst of un- sound mind."
ST. HELENS REVISION COURT.
CATHOLIC PRIFSTS AND THEIR VOTES.
LIBERAL RESULT OF THE REVISION.

An interesting point was raised at Monday's sit- ting of the St. Helens Revision Court,presided over by Mr. J. T. Foard, revising barris'er. Mr. J. Barn, representing the I iberals, had objected in court to the names of Joseph Booth and Alfred Mottram Booth being retained on the lists, the qualification being put down as "dwelling-house (joint), 40, Knowsley- road." 'I he Revising Barrister held there was no such qualification as "dwelling-house joint," and one of the names must come off. The name of Joseph Booth was accordingly struck off. Mr. Swift,who represented the Conservatives,and had been absent when the question was raised, afterwards complained that Mr. Bain had been objocting behind his back. Be contended that the revising barrister had no right to strik.: Mr. Both off, A dwelling-house joint was not a disqualification if the property was rated 3 t a sufficient value to allow £lO for each vote.

Mr. Bain referred to 30 and 31 Victoria, chap. 102 section 3, which dealt with household franchise,and pro- vided that no man should he entitled to be registered,as a voter by reason of his being a joint occupier of any dwelling-house. The-Revising Barrister agreed with this view, and Later in the day Mr. Swift, during the reading of the lists, referred to the names of ten priests who appeared on the East Sutton Ward List in respect ef joint occupa- tion of the monastery connected with St. Anne's Catholic Church. Mr. Bain contended that it was not a similar ease to that of Booth, and cited the case of Meyler r. Metcalfe. which, he said, covered it. That was the case of a Roman Catholic priest and seven curates occupying a house built by the parishioners tor the residence of their clergy, and conveyed to trustees, by whose permission the voters occepied. Mr. Bain further submitted that inasmuch as each priest. had the exclusive use of a room they were entitled to vote under section 5. chapter 26,0 f 41 and 42 Victoria,which Set forth :—" Where an occu- pier is entitled to the sole and exclusive use of any part of a house, that part shall not be deemed to be occupied otherwise than pep irately by reason only that the occu- pier is entitled to the Fent USA of some other part." The Revising Barrister said he must have some proof that the premises were so occupied, or he would strike them off. Mr. Bain said he did not think that it was fair that so many votes should be struck off the lists without some notice of objection had been given by the revising bar- rister to the persons concerned, and suggested that his Honour should adjourn the case until the following day, and then al'ow it to he fully discussed. The Revising Barrister said he could not adjourn it, and he must striks off nine of the ten names, only one being allowed to remain. The Rev Richard Foy was allowed the vote,he having been resident at the Monastery the longest time, and the following were taken off :—Revs. Daniel Nugent, Emidus Smith, Paulinus Barton, Francis Kelly, Malachy Gavin, Aloysi us O'Brien. Ii lephonsus I tcdonald, E,g iii Wilkes, and Pacificus M•Manus Steward. For the same reason the Revs. George Dover and Timothy Courtenay were strut k off in respect of the Presbytery connected with Holy Cross Catholic Church, and the name of the Rev. Joseph Gradwell was allowed to remain. Mr. Bain e.alled attention to the names of Mr. William Pilkington, Roby Hall; Mr. rhos. Pilkington, Knowsley Cottage, Prescot ; Mr. Wm. Windle Pilkington, The Hasels,Prescot ; Mrs Richard Pilkington, Rsinford Hall ; Mr. William Lee Pilrington,Huyton Grange, Huyton ; and Mr. George Herbert Pilkington, Wheathill, Roby, all of which appeared the VC, st Sutton list twice, the quali- fications being " works (j ,lot) and offices successive " and "works (jt int) and house, luncheon room, and cafe t joint)." It apnearea that the whole of the gentle- men had been on the list in previous years in respect of the glass works, hut, during the past year they had formed themselves into a limited eornpany,and therefore could not he on for the works. It was stated that each of the gentlemen named had reserved a eepasite office which had not been sold to the compeny. The offiees were of suffisient rateable value to sew the votes. „d his Honour decided to t-,k elf the names on the second qualification and allow tit in to stand for "works (joint) and offices."

div.head: BESS I ONS.
div.p: BESS I ONS.
AN OFF-WINE LICENSE GRANTED._

These adjourned sessions were held on Monday morning at the Court tiouse, Runcorn, Messrs. Jno. Brundrit and T. Rigby being t he justices. The only case down for hearing was a renewed application by Mr. J. Burton. for an ti'f-wi'ne license at 27, and 29, Bridge-street, in the oame of Mr. Wm. Edgar Lea, joint executor, with Mr. Marston. to the late Mr. Isaac Speakman. who, during his lifetime, had carried on the present business of chemist and druggist. Mr. Burton explained thit he had applied for the license at the last annual licensing session, but it was tl en adjourned in order to issue fresh notices and to make the application in Mr. L-a's name only,as their worsh,ps had thought it would be improper to issue a license to two executors. The neces,ary notices had been issued, and if there were no objections to Mr. Lea's name, he would ask that the license be granted to him. The issue of the required notices having been proved, Mr. Burton asked the Superintendent if he had any objection to offer against the name of Mr. Loa. .The Superintendent answered in the negative, but remarked that to him the license did not appear necessary inasmuch as there v ere several wine-retailing places near to the shop. Next door there was a wine and spirit store, and across the road was an hotel. He did not think, however, that there was any obj.,ction against the four qualifying points advanced by Mr. Burton. The license was granted.

div.head: VICTIM oF VA.CCINATION.
div.p: A VICTIM oF VA.CCINATION.

As there is no evil without its remedy, se there is no boon that does not carry some compensating disadvan- tage. It is a boon to live in an enlightened country, where the health of the people is the care of the law. The law requires that all children be vaccinated. This is a precaution that is sometimes attended by unfortu- nate evils, and the following interesting item shows what these are, and also how thy may he remedied. Mrs. Nixon, of Woodbine-cottage, Springwell, Dur- ham, thus described a misfortune which seemed to date frc,m the vaccination of her child to a "Durham Chronicle" reporter: My baby is eleven months old. Up to three months old he was healthy. He was vacci- nated, and a decline in health dated from that time. He lost appetite and became very peevish. The doctor des- cribed the illness as spasmodic croup. Some ,of the neighbours said my boy had the rickets. At eight months old he commenced to have fits. The doctor gave little hope. He did say, if he got over his first year he might get well, but frotn the shake of the head with which this was imparted, he did not entertain very strong hopes, and I prepared myself for the worst. For three or four days at one time he was dreadfully ill, and during twenty-seven hours went into no less than four- teen fits. I was despairing, when I was told, by Mrs. Lisle in the village of the wonderful cure which had been wrought upon her baby by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. I asked her about her baby's illness and cure. The case seemed so like my baby's, I wrote for a box, and am heartily thankful I did, for, without doubt, they saved the life of my boy when all else seemed unavailing." The mother showed a round-limbed, chubby-faced, rosy baby, as healthful as it was playful. Re-opening the conversation, the reperter observed that pills seemed to be queer medicine for babies, and asked how they had been administered.
"I gave him one every day in two doses, cutting a pill in half, and dissolving it in warm water. The change for the better was noticeable almost directly."

div.head: RUNCORN REVISION COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN REVISION COURT.

Mr. David Archer Vaiv.zhati Colt Williams, re- vising barristtr for the North wich Pant amentary Division of Cheshire, opened the revision of voter's lists of Runcorn and outlying townshil.s on Friday morning at the Runcorn Police Court. Mr. William ! Handley, Runcorn, appeared for the Liberals, and the Conservatives were represented by Mr. C, J. Hughes, of Northwich. The lists from the various townships with- in the polling districts of Aston-by• Sutton, Halton and Weston, were first dealt with, the work of revising them b-ing of a very routine nature, involving no points of interest. Shortly after beginning business, the revising barrister observed that on the Aston list he noticed that the vote of the Rev. Cann Maitland Wood was objected to. Mr. Robinson, overseer for Sutton, intimated that the objection was his. The Rev. Canon Woed was not rated nor had he ask .d to be rated. Claims had been made by the rev. gentleman for Acton and Aston Grange, but he was not rated in either township.—The revising ha rrister : " It is tithe rent I suppose.—Mr. Handley : Yes, sir.—Replying to further questions by the barrister Mr. Robinson stated that Canon Wood had escaped rating because theamount was so small that it was not w rth rating and probably not worth collecting. The tithe rent charge belonged to Christ Church, Oxford.— Mr. Acton, assistant overseer for Sutton, remarked that the tithe had been demanded but no one would pay.— Mr. Hughes intimated that he had claimed for a number of townships for the rev. gentleman as the latter did not know in which he was rated.—Mr. Handley said that an occupation qualification was sought. An occupier of tithes, if there was such a thing, was to be assessed to all local rates.—The claim was disallowed. In the afternoon the Runcorn lists were taken, the revision of these lasting until the following morning. Nothing of interest transpired, and at the conclusion of business Mr. Handley thanked the -revising barrister on behalf of Mr. Hughes and himself for the kind, and courteous nay in which he bad conducted the proceed- ings. It was the sincere wish of both Mr. Hughes and himself that he would long be spared to revise the lists of that division.—ln response, the hiarrister thaeked the agents in return for their kind expressions and assistance. Without their help it would have been impossitlie for him to have got through the work. He also spoke highly of the way in tahicli the Runcorn lists bad been prepared. Be had rarely revised a more perfect set, and this fact reflected much credit upon the over,eer and his assistant whose work it was to draw them up.

so liberally adorned. Often, just at the critical moment of staying, to prevent this arboreal en- tancilement, the fitful breeze would change its mind and the tack upon which you are standing instantly to the opposite one,reneering a slight col- lision inevitable. Out of .this poor" Tem " would creep ignobly with his decks littered with leaves, dead boughs, and other unnautical debris. In this intermittent mode we workee our way up the river to Eccleston Ferry where, as the evening was gett- ing advanced we cast out the emblem, and retained the hope of security thereby. Then, after a slight refection, we sought the inner recesses of the "tub" while the river flowed silently by and the eternal stars with Chaldean memories kept the silent watches of the night. So, content with this super- vision, we ducked. and, like Jack-in-the-box, put down the lid. The experiences of the next day (Wednesday) was little else but a repetition of our first, with the difficulties rather intensified by the narrowing stream and the more overhanging trees. Add to this the ever increasing strength of the cur- rent as we got higher rendered this part of the trip a test of the relative strength of our patience and endurance and the increasing prepondrence of the adverse circumstances. New we had to hold on to a bush on the weather side of the river to allow a passing rain-storm to go over without drenching us then we had to make shortened tacks to avoid partly submerged snaggs. In this way we won our way until some mile or so above the confluence of the river Alyn where the river got so narrow and the adverse turnings so frequent, that patience gave way and we reversed, tack and tack to Eaton,where, as Di said, we took house next door to the Duke, after pushing our boat further up that river than ever a boat of that size and progression had been before, or at least, for the last thousand years. (To be Concluded)

div.head: DI. OS THE DEE RE-VISITED.
div.p: DI. OS THE DEE RE-VISITED.
BY MR. JOHN PEERS.

In fulfilment of a promise made, I started, one bright Tuesday morning, overland for Chester, to explore with Di. the upper reaches of the Dee. For my friend had formed and cultivated the ambition to push his " tub " further up the winding reaches of the river tout ever was craft of her size and sort before. So here this bright and breezy morning found me on tramp to Widnes, and by bridge to Runcorn, thence by train to Sutton Weaver. Now, the meteorological description I have indulged in applies—be it noted—only to the walking part of this excursion to Sutton Weaver. When in the train the gathering clouds foretold by their ominous um- brageousnesa the fate which actually met me when I alighted at the station ti begin my walk to Ches- ter. The wind was strong and and gusty, while the rain came down like bedclothes—in sheets and wet blankets for pleasure seekers. Crouching beneath the imperfect shelter of a bush, with the pros- pect of walking some 12 or 13 miles through half liquid mud to sit in a damp boat, was an infliction I wished to avoid, so I sped through the deluge to the nearest station—llalton--and there found—besides the welcome shelter—that I had time to kick my heels for near two mortal hours. Exhilarating prospect I Wonder what is the proportion of suicides among wayside station masters. Greatly admire, too their moral force which enables so many of them to resist the fatal facility of the next express to terminate the pro- longed miseries which go near to drive to distraction the less indurated but intransient traveller. Truly here was a fine end put to the glorious anticipations of the morn ! .Sic transit gloria mundi ! I need not write it as the cobbler would have it, after keeping St. Monday—not wisely but too well—Sie transit gioria Monday. Howbeit, just as visions of a speedy exit per next express—as a relief, not with it .but by it; the station master renewed within my bosom that " hope which sets the captive free," by the in- formation that an earlier train might be caught at Frodsham. Having been caught in the rain, catch- ing this train was thought preferable to catching cold and the dumps by further sojourn where Jupiter Pluvius had stationed me. Of course when seated in the train the weather cleared up. ,So like our perverse insular climate. However I let the weather shine away as liked it best, I was not going to humour its whims and get out and walk, not I. Alighting in Chester and stoutly resisting the ROWS of attractions it presents to arrest the curious visitor, [soon found myself upon the light suspen- sion bridge which spans the river above the weir. From this commanding attitude I soon picked out the white-hulled " Bowling" moored to some steps opposite Mr. Capner's boat stage. Getting abreast of tte boat I found my philosophic friend, if not "on hospitable thoughts intent," at least intent upon the preparations fora "dine." He had got to the potato-boiling stage of that operation. While this was in progress Di. dilated upon the manitold virtues of red-kidneys. To hear him talk there was only one potato and Di was its prophet; any way Di. profited by the potatoes. Dinner over we decided—that is Di. decided and I acquiesced—to weigh and proceed up the river on our exploring expedition. But ere this I pleasant anticipation could be fulfilled sea stores— or river stores if you will—must be laid in. Tis I ever so ! Though " Ev'n in our ashes live their wonted fires," a little fuel this flame requires. Toe sublime and the beautiful cannot be studied except from a material basis! Ichabod I What a drop ! from the sublime and beautiful to bacon collops and rei kidneys. Here let the reader return thanks unto Di., in that his impatience to be off has pre- vented the indulgence of a wild desire I feel for an exeursus into the theme of the close connection there exists between matter and spirit. Possibly the reader has no mind to go into this matter? Never mind, its no matter. Away then we sped before the still strong gale, up the lower and much be- sculled reaches, glad to get away from the more hackneyed bits of the river, where inexperienced oarsmen so manipulate as to run into the dangers they seek to avoid. Past larger and more pretentious house boats than Di.'s, but of the ignoble apteral type, inert, and ignominiously moored stem and stern to restraining trees. Alas! poor "Bowling I" And is it thy fate to consort with such tame inanimates, upon the insipid waters of this placid river? Thou, who's elight erst it was to brave the bristling crests of the salt seas ; and rejoice in the merry melody of the whistling winds, whose shrill diapason accorded so well with the screaming sea- gull's wilder note ! For thee no 'more the music of the surge, No more thy counter the ruddy. fire shall. grace. No more past f. Thy prow w
le race.
I proved no lagl

What boots it viands at more per pound Are at thy present owner's bid ? Can these compare with the erst sweet sound, Of curling, kippers on the ready grin ? How are the mighty fallen ! From being the honoured habitation of an aquatic philosopher to come to-but let me not ant.icipate but proceed. Now the wind was high and right merrily did we progress where the high wind came low enough to affect us. With a clear space over the meadows to windwards, where the wind could get at us, old " Tom " careened to the breeze down to the lee scuppers and, in occasional gusts, deck-in he scurried along with a great "bone in his teeth " in a way calculated to unnerve the timid naiads of this placid stream. Anon we should come to a place o'er hung by trees where scarce a breath of the roaring breeze above us found its ineffectual way and the water looked like glass, until an eddying gust, born of the backward currents from the trees, came rip- pling on the waters and carried us some little on our way, to leave us with idly shaking sails, los- ing the little god its capricious favour had bestowed. One minute we should be in the "dol- drums" with the mainsail hanging straight from gaff to boom, listening, with aggravated patience, to the waste of roaring winds still bowing the trees aloft; cthen with a vicious rush the eddy would be upon us again and away we sped for a while upon the other tack. Splenuid practice this for him who ' wants to improve his touch upon the tiller! Every cat's-paw must be watched and every coquetting zephyr courted that promises impelment. And, while one eye must be to weather, the other needs to be aloft to avoid undue interference with over- hanging boughs, with which these grassy banks are

div.head: WATER POLO AT WARRINGTON BATHS.
div.p: WATER POLO AT WARRINGTON BATHS.

At the Corporation Baths, Legh-street, on Monday night, the semi-final, for the Liverpool and District Cup, water polo competition was played between , Warrington and Southport and a club handicap of two lengths of the bath was swain off in five heats. In the first three heats there were only two entries in each. P. Furness winning the first, W. D. Sutton the second, and W. Owen the third. A rather better show was made in the last two heats, there being four entries in the fourth heat, which was wan by C. Russell, and five in the last heat, won by W. Ashton. The first in each heat had to swim in the final, in which Furness was first, Ashton second, and Russell third. Here it was announced that the Southport team had been delayed on the way and in order to fill in the time it was decided to give an exhibition polo match by the second team. Fair Turner officiated as referee in this match. The two sides were distinguished by blue and white caps. After some very amusing scrambling the score stood at half time ;-- Blues 2 goals to nil. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A WARRINGTON

div.head: TRADESItAN'S WIFE.
div.p: TRADESItAN'S WIFE.

Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy county coroner, held an inquest at the Parade room of the Police Station, on the body of Mary Scotson, wife of James Scot son, 8, Bold-street, wine and spirit merchant,:who died on Monday morning from injuries received by fall- ing down the cellar steps the previous day. James Scotson said that his wife as 52 years of age. She had been in delicate health for some time, caused by her own habits—she having been intemperate. On Sun- day witness went to church at 10 30 a.m., and his wife was then in her usual health, and was sober. When he got home at about 12.30,he found her lying upon the sofa bleeding from a wound in the back of her head. She said something to him but het could not catch what it was. She never spoke afterwards. Dr. Starkey Smith was sent for and attended her to the time of her aeath, early on Monday morning. Eleanor Scotson, daughter of the deceased, said that her mother and herself remained at home on Sunday , morning. Witness had occasion to leave for three or ! four minutes, and when she returned, her mother had gone out of the kitchen. Witness and Eleanor Gibson, a servant went to look for her, and they found her ly- ing, at the bottom of the cellar stairs. Witness then went for a neighbour, Mrs. Critchley, and also for Dr. Braide who however was not at home. She then waited for her father. Her mother never spoke when they found her. There was no handrail on the stairs, and the cellar WS dark. Eleanor Gibson gave corroborative evidence and also said that deceased was sober. Witness and Mrs. Critchley carried deceased up the stairs into the kitchen while the last witness went for the doctor The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental Death."

div.head: SECRETARY'S REPORT.
div.p: SECRETARY'S REPORT.

The SECRETARY (Mr. W. E.Atkin) read the following report :—During the past season the society carried out the work proposed in the prospectus 'issued last Novem- ber under immense d;ffieulties, but the two concerts given on Dt-cember 12, 1893, and A.,ril 3, 1894, were successful performances, and reflect nothing hut credit on the members arid their indefatigable conductor, and the only thing to be regretted is that the treasurer can ' not, I fear, report a like success in respect of both these concerts. When, besides providing for the proper per- formance of the works attempted, a society (with a totally inadequate subscription list) has to furnish ,heat, decorate, and almost literally build its concert hall, and quite literally erect its own platform, that society can- not,l think, very confidently look forward to handsome profits, and the wonder to my mind is that the War- rington Musical Society has not found itself in still greater difficulties at the end of the season 1893-4 than it most unfortunately is actually involved in now. Some- thing must he done, and I want to impress upon every single individual member that the debt is the society's debt. It is not Mr. Reynolds' debt, or fry debt, nor Mr. Crossley's, nor the private affair and spscial perquisite of the committee. It has been incurred in part by un- fortunate losses on concerts given by the society as a body. Ido not mean to s-iy that the society is totally indifferent, but a very large proportion of the members are satisfied that having paid their 2s. 6d. subscription they have done all they can towards supporting the society financially. Quite possibly many may have paid as much money as they can afford for one season. By, the way, it is something like id. per rehearsal and con- ' certs thrown in at 2s. 61. per member. Still that is not the question. lam certain that many members might do much, very much more than they do to support the society, by advertising its ends and aims,influencing the public generally to support it, and making its success a more personal interest. Our concert subscription list ought to he three times the length it is, and I am con- vinced that by a coestant canvassing during the season, a society mustering in members as strong numerically as yours does could have a much larger number of out- side supporters did everyone do their- best in the way I mean. Thus while thanking the section which has always done its best in this way—and such thanks are due also from the whole society—let me at the same , time ask the much larger section, which I cannot help feeling has always been unthinkingly content to be more or less inactive in this direction, to stir up and do like- wise. I have with regret to report the sad death of our flute player, which occurred during the past season ; and also regret to hear that Mr. Roberts, our leader, is in bad health.and cannot join us for the coming season. The season opened October Bth, 1893, and closed with the final concert, April 3, 1894. In conclusion, he said he had no intention in what he had said to hurt the feel- ings of anyone, he only desired that all the members would take a personal interest •in the welfare of the society. (Applause.) TREASURER'S REPORT.

The TREASURER (Mr. L. W. Reynolds) also submitted his report for the year. He said it would probably be in the rec64llection of most of thew that their last annual meeting was held in May of last year, and beirg early the accounts were not closed for the season 1892-93, therefore the statement of accounts submitted to the meeting was only an approximate one. The estimated balance against the society at that time was stated to be something apprnaching £5O. He was glad to say that at the assets stated at that time as owing to the society were realised. On the other hand, rather more liability was against the society than was estimated in conse- quence of some of the accounts not having come in, so that the actual result at the end of the season 1892-3 was rather worse than was stated at the last geneial meet- ing. The amount actually was £52 104. 51. The ex- penditure for the oast year had been £155124. 11d., and the income £lO3 3s. 4d., leaving a balance on the wrong side of £52 94. 7d., which with the adverse balance of the previous year gave the total loss to the society of £lO5. This money had all been drawn from the bank by himself, and the interest would have to be paid on it by somebody. The subscription list was only £52 ss. from the two concerts they gave last season, and he found that during the seties of 12 years ending 1889 the subscription list for the same number of concerts varied from £ll5 to £145. This was double the amount sub- scribed at the present time.
The reports were adopted. ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

Mr. Jour; WHITE proposed the re-election of Mr. John Rvlands as president, and spoke of him as the father of music in Warrington. As long as he lived he trusted that they would be unanimous in placing him in that position, so long as he was willing to occupy it. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. R. T. Faircloug,h seconded the motion and it was carried with acclamation.—The Chairman, in responding, said lie was afraid it was a very poor reason to say that because he had been connected with the society for a long time that he was all the more useful. He hoped he should be of some use to them in the com- ing year, which he thought would he the most difficult year they had . ever had. (Applause.)—All the vice- pres'dants were elected, and the name of Captain Edelsten was added.—The Chairman proposed the re- . election of the Secretary, Mr. Atkin, and that a vote of thanks be accorded him for his services, remarking that he was one of the best seeretaries they had ever had.— Mr.R. fl.Silc.nck seconded, and the motion was carried.— On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. New- combe, Mr. Reynolds' the treasurPr, was re-elected and he was thanked fnr his past services.—Mr. Newcombe was elected auditor, and the committee were re-elected. Mr. ATKIN, in responding to the vote of thanks, spoke about the posf ion of the society. He said it would be impossible to give any concerts this year, hut at the same time he hoped sornelhing would be done to relieve thp society of debt. He also thought that the organist, Mr.G F.F. White, librarian, Mr. Crassley,the leader, and Mr. Woods sulitoraleservel their thanks.and he proposed a vote of thanks to them.—The motion was agreed to. —Mr. Rylands said that. the woik Mr. Crossley ha.l done in connection with that society had been extraordinary, and the results had also been in keeping with it. He was pleased to support the vote of thanks, and also to request him to accept the ntfiee of conductor for the ensuing year.—Mr. Crossley, in responding to the vote of thanks, said it appeared clear to everyone, after the experience of the last two seasons, that they could give no more concerts until they got the use of the new hall that was being presented to the town by Mr. Parr. At the same time, the commit'..ee were quite of opinion, with himself, that there must be .no idea of dropping practices. (Hear, hear.) He, therefore, proposed that , they begin their praritices next Tuesd Ir. (Hear, hear.) A desultory discussion took place with regard to the question of providing ways and means to clear off the debt on the societv.—Mr. John White suggested that a musical converiaziene should he arranged, and further pointed out that it was very likely the society would he invited to take part in the opening of the new Public Will in March next.—The Secretary meis- tinned that Mr. J. C. Parr was very favourably inclined to the society.—The Chairman remarked that the trea- surer's report might have been worse. If they considered the position they had been in it was wonderful that it was not worse.. They could not expect the public to sub- scribe to the society in the position it had been in. They had no hall or comfortable place to gives concertip. He proposed a vote of thanks to the Secretary and Treasurer. (Applsose.)—Mr. NEWCOMBE seconded, aril the vote was passed unanimensly.—lt was decided, in pursuance of a sugget:tion thrown out by the President, that an addi- tional committee should be appointed, and four ladies and the same number of gentlemen were selected to form this committee. The following are the names of the Committee :—Mrs. James Fairclough, Mrs. Atkin Mrs. John Rocnolds, and Mrs. L. J. T. Da.rwall. Rev. L. J_ T. Darwali, Rev. J. E. Forbes, and Councillor R. T. Fairclough, and Mr. W. S. Howard.--A vote of I thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close.
