Gothenburg As we anticipited last week, . versus attempts have been made to show Local Option. that Mr. GLADSTONE'S• letter in favour of the Gothenburg system of licensing discredits local option. But the attempts have not been successful. It is seen clearly enough that there is no necessary antagonism between the Gothenburg plan of dealing with public-houses and local option. The one means a change of the present licensing system, and the other the giving of a majority of the inhabitants in any particular locality power to say whether or not they will have public-houses in their midst upon any terms. As Mr. WHYTE, Secretary of the United Kingdom Alliance, explains in a letter to the "Daily Chronicle," local optionists have never claimed that the passing of the Lbcal Option Bill would be a complete remedy for the evils of the drink . traffic. Local option is a long way from total prohibition which is the goal aimed at by most pronounced temperance reformers. At the same time it seems quite clear that the Bailor of CHESTER'S scheme is not of itself, a complete remedy. As Mr. WILYTII points out, in Norway where public-house reform of the character advocated by the Bishop has been more thoroughgoing and more succesful than anywhere else, the necessity for prohibition continues to be strongly felt; and it appears that the legislature has already supple.. mented the Gothenburg Act by a measure of local option, in other words, giving localities the power to totally prohibit the traffic. From this it would seem that the Gothenburg system andlocal option are not only not antagonistic but are actually ' supplemental of each other—that one is incomplete without the other. In one respect all this discus- sion of licensing and kindred matters must givis satisfaction to those who are interested in temper ance reforms. It proves conclusively that the question is a "live" one which can be no longer ignored or put on one side.

Our Member. Where is the member for War- rington ? One hears on all hands of members of Parliament addressing their consti- tuents and giving an account of their steward- ship, but. Warrington is completely neglected by Mr. PlERronrr. Of course there are some excuses. From a Tory point of view, the last session of Parliament was not a brilliant affair. The Govern- ment managed to pass some useful measures, but the record of the Opposition is that of barren and factious obstruction. And even in the game of obstruction Mr. PlEEPoirrr personally played only an extremely minor part. 'Still, there is foreign politics to fall back upon, and the member for Warrington has a weakness for enlarging upon the "integrity of this gi eat empire." Did he not tell us a year or two ago that • there were no Radicals east of Gibraltar A man had only to leave the bracing atmosphere of English freedom,and dwell amongst the effemin- ate and ignorant natives of the Rot to become a good Tory. We may remind Mr. Piaarourr „ that the present is an admirable time for aa exposition of foreign affairs. The question of Madagascar is, for ibistance, coming to the front. Lord SALISBURY, that spirited foreign minister who can always be relied upon to look after the interests of his native land, entered into a bargain by which the French were to have a free hand with regard to Madagascar, and they now seem to be disposed to take advantage of that bargain in a way which will very seriously injure British trade and influence in the E tst. But, in any case,he ought really to let us have the benefit of his impassioned oratory some time during the recess. A member of Parliament has his responsibilities as well as his privileges.

TIM question of railway rates is Railway Rates. again being a good deal discussed in different parts of the country, and some re- markable instances of the special rates which the railway companies give to f,reign produce have been mentioned. For example, one correspondent of a daily newspaper mentions that the rate on sugar from Hamburg to Manchester by way of Hull has been reduced to lrs. 3d., including delivery in Manchester, while the local rate from Hull to Manchester remains at 15s. 10d., or 7d. per ton more than the through rate. This is encouragement of foreign industry with a vengeance. If the Germans do not run their British competitors off the field they certainly can- not blaine the patriotic British railway directors for not giving them due facilities. In regard to garden and farm produce the rates in certain parts of the country are practically prohibitory,and producers are, in some instances, allowing their crops of fruit and vegetables to go to waste rather than pay the exorbitant demands for carriage. It does not do in all cases to accept even as a gift a large quantity of fruit if the railway companies are to have a hand in the delivery. A story has just been told by another correspondent of a large fruiterer in the South of England who accepted a gift of sixty bushels of apples from relatives in Sornersetshire. He naturally thought that the transaction would be a profitable one, but when he came to reckon with the railway company, he • found that he could have bought the same quantity of foreign apples in his own locality for less money that he had to pay for the carriage of oi the English commodity.

OSMAN, While acting as the Mandi's chief lieutenant, was., it will be remembered, killed at frequent intervals, and for the last month or more the " collapse " of the strike has been announced at least three times a week in some of the daily papers, yet there is a Strike still. Trio Scotch miners have displayed a capacity for combination and a determination Which their employers did not anticipate. They have been badly led, as their leaders have wasted energies in squabbling amongst themselves which Ahould have been devoted to the promotion of the cause they had in hand, and this is mostly respon- ilible for the partial breakdown which took place a fortnight ago. Whatever may be the ultimate result of the struggle so far as wages are concerned, the Scotch mineowners must surely by this time have seen the folly of the position they took up at the commencement. The time has now gone by when huge trade unions such as the kiners' Federation can he ignored as though they had no existence. The miners are entitled to ccmbine, and, when combined,they are entitled to ask that their grievances, real or imaginary, shal he listened to even though they be formulated %rough the trade union officials. To decline even to meet the meri's leaders was a display of arro- gance on the part of the coalowners which seems gcnost grotesque at this time of day.

AT the Conference of Sanitary " Squalid Cots and Homes." Inspectors held in Liverpool on Tuesday, Dr. VACKER, of Birken- head, gave the inspectors a suggestive piece of lidvice. It was this: that the inspectors should do their utmost to conserve their health by living either in the suburbs or right out in the 13untry, and so counteract the influence of the bad atmosphere of the squalid cots and homes among which they had to spend their working liours." No one will disoute the wisdom of the

counsel so far as the sanitary inspectors themselves 4r. e concerned. It was good sound advice and the Inspectors would, no doubt, do well to act upon it. ilut the question which arises is—what about the People who spend in "the bad atmosphere of the liqualid cots and homes" not only their working hotirs, but practically all the hours of their lives? 1,-

What state of physical, mental and moral health Ilte they to preserve? The slums and " insani- ,tary areas" which are still allowed to exist in ittrge English towns must be bad indeed when ltdvice of this sort has to be given to the inspectors 'Whose duty it is to make occasional visits to %era.

PROPOSED CYCLE PARADE AT RUNCORN. Runcorn cyclists are considering whether to hold a lantern parade and fancy carnival shortly for the benefit of some philanthropic institution, and with the object of making the necessary arrangements a meeting of cyclists was held on Thursday evening. Unfortunately, how- ever, owing to the very sparse attendance of outsiders willing to help,the matter was deferred to a future meet- ing, when it is hoped the public will show a little more enthusiasm with regard to the proposAl. There was no lack of interest on the part of the cyclists, all of whom are only too ready to make the affair a success. MORE HELP TOWARDS THE RUNCORN TECHNICAL INSTITUTE. It is pleasing to announce that an additional subscrip- tion has recently been received towards the building fund of the Runcorn Technical Institute. The donors are Messrs. Charles Taylor and Co., timber merchants, Liverpool, and the amount of the gift is £lO. The total subscriptions received, practically amount to £5OO. so that the building committee may now approach Mr.J.T. Brunner, M.P. for the fulfilment of his promise of £5OO. Mr. Brunner's intended visit co Runcorn on Wednesday might probably serve as a fitting opportunity to present to him the state of the exchequer.

RUNCORN WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION. Under the auspices of this organization a temperance mission was held on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. and Thursday evenings, in the Bethesda Lecture Hall, Ron- corn. On each occasion an address was delivered by Mrs. Metcalfe, of Burnley, illustrative of the evils attending habits of intemperance. This lady dealt with several phases of the temperance question, and some of her remaiks elicited loud plaudits from her audience who evidently highly appreciated her style. The pro- ceedings each evening were enlivened by the perform- ance of a musical programme,Miss Clara Taylor,R.A.M., Miss A.M.Taylor, Mr. and Mrs. Burn, and Miss Heather- ington being amongst the artistes.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, RUNCORN. In another column will be found an announcement that harvest thanksgiving services will be held on Sun- day next in zonnection with the above place of wor- ship in Greenway-road. fhe Rev. W. Albert, of Wins- ford, the late pastor of the Greenway-road chapel, has been secured to preach in the morning and evening, whilst the Rev. J. Stafford, Methodist Free Church minister, will deliver an address in the afternoon. Special musical selections will be contributed by the choristers, and the proceeds are on behalf of the church fund. On Monday evening there will be a coffee sup- per in the schoolroom. It is hoped that the congrega- tions will be large and the donations liberal. QUARTERLY MEETING OF THE RUNCORN IA ESLEYAN CIRCUIT. _ _ _

On Monday afternoon tile quarterly meeting of the Runcorn Wesleyan Circuit was held in the Brunswick vestry, the Rev. W. Brackenhury occupying the chair. There were also present the Revs. W. George, and W. L. Stone, Messrs. E. Taylor, R.Rawlinson (circuit stewards), and J M. Frith, secretary.—in official welcome was extended to the newly-appointed ministers to which the Chairman responded expressing the belief that in the order of providence they had been sent there, and added that it would be their earnest endeavour to do their duty in the circuit for their Lord and Master.—The stewards presented the financial statement which was most satisfactory considering the extraordinary expendi- ture incurred during the past quarter through the removal of the three ministers and the preparation of the residences for their successors. The balance on the adverse side amounted to only £l3 —The superintend- ent minister gave a record of the society members which showed a slight increase on the previous quarter. At the request of the chairman, the Rev.W. George gave the details of the new legislation passed at the recent conference sp(cially affecting junior society classes and Sunday School representation on the Central Board.— Mr. J. R. Frith, treasurer of the Foreign Missicns was thanked for his services and re-elected for another year. The Rev. W. George and Mr.E. Taylor were re-appointed secretaries, and representatives were chosen from all the other societies in the circuit to form a committee for the ensuing year. div.p: BURTON WOOD SCHOOL BOARD.

The quarterly meeting of the above was held in the plass-room of the Board Schools, Burtonwood, on Tuesday evening, when there were present, Messrs. Wm. Fairclough and Thomas Norcott, Rev. A. M. Mitchell, H. Gawthorpe (school master), Wm. Webster (clerk). Letters of apology having been read from the chairman and vice-chairman, Mr. Win. Fairclough was elected to the chair. The correspondence of the month was considered. The Clerk reported the receipt since last meeting of drawing grant, .£4 45.; proceeds of books sold, 9s 4d.; proceeds of needlework sold, 3s. 41. Accounts and salaries amounting to £93 2s. 44., were passed for payment. The estimates for the coming six months were considered and a precept for £llO, being a rate of 11d. in the .£, was drawn en the overseers. A schedule of duties of caretaker and cleaner was settled, and it was resolved in con- sideration af more frequent cleanings required, to increase the school cleaner's salary, but to require her to provide all brushes and materials necessary to perform her duties satisfactorily. The attendance was considered. The resignations of Mr. Albert Hewitt (assistant master), and Mr. John Forster, who has acted as school attendance officer since July, 1877, were received.

div.head: SIN GULAR DISPUTS As TO PROPERTY.
div.p: SIN GULAR DISPUTS As TO PROPERTY.

At tict;—"Niarrington. County Court, on Thursday, his Honour Deputy-Judge Crawford gave judgment in the case of John Haselden, James Haselden, and Wm. Haselden v. Thomas Larkin. The plaintiffs, for whom Mr. Riley, of St. Helens, appeared,claimed (as surviving executors of the late John Haselden, of Blacicbrook, Haydock), from the defendant, the sum of .£9 is. ld, for rent of a dwelling-house at Blackbrook,and also possession of the clttage itself. It appears that the testator left by his will one of his cottages to each of his four eons; the cottage occupied by the defendant, Larkin, being left to , Peter Haselden,since deceased. For four years after the testator's death the rents were collected by a rent collector, and divided at the end of every month, but on Peter's death his eldest son John then took possession of Larkin's house and himself received Larkin's rent. The plaintiffs as surviving executors served Larkin, through their solicitor, with a notice to pay his rent to them but this was disputed by J)lin Hasel- den (Peter's son) who continued to collect the rent. The question for his Honour to determine was whether the property passed direct to Peter Hasel- den and his children, or whether the property be- longed to the executors until such time as all debts owing by the estate were paid, and all expenses incidental to the proving of the will. Mr. Riley said that John Haselden the grandson of the testa- tor would not go into the accounts and do what the executors thought was right. Mr. Longton for the defence argued that the will completely transferred the property in Larkin's house over to the son Peter and his children and that they were justified in now (Injecting the rent independently of the ex- ecutors. He (Mr. Longton) said that any claim that the executors might have, should he' made against, Peter Haselden's representatives and not against. Larkin who had paid all his rent up to the present time and was therefore an innocent party. After . considerable a rgument on both sides his Honour said that the executors had assented to the bequest of Larkin's house to the deceased Peter,and that therefore the present action must fall, but he expressed the hope that the parties would he able to amicably settle any accounts which they had be- tween them.
QUARTERLY MEETING OF THE RUNCORN SONS OF THYPERANCR.

The quarterly meeting of this society was held on Saturd4y evening last in Greenway-road School. Mr. George Sutton in the chair. The sick stewar is, Messrs. J. Johnson and T. J. Holt presented a very interesting report from which it appeared tnat out of a membership of 280, adults 34 had received £43 7s. 6d. against £56 13i 6 I. in the corresponding period of last qtrirter. This was considered a very favourable state ot affairs. On the motion of Mr. Thomas Holt, seconded by Mr. Thomas Clarke, it was decided to pay the annual sub- scription of one guinea to the nurse fund. An interest- ing convers tion ensued on the beneficial work performed by the nurse, many members expressing the opinion that it was a CliriA-like work and not confined to p Arty sect, or creed, and that the C tmmittee were worthy of high praise in their labour of love.

EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The quarterly society tea and meeting were held in the Lecture Hall of the Wesleyan Chapel on Wednesday evening. There were about 100 persons present to tea, which was presided over by the lady members of the congregation. The attendance at the after meeting was much augmented, the chair being occupied by the Rev. R. Bartley, resident minister. In addition to talking over the affairs of the church, occasion was taken to tender a hearty welcome to the new pastor, the Rev. It. Bartley, addresses being given by the learlers of the society, ineuding Messrs. J. Roberts, P. Parr, Gosling, &a.
LANCASHIRE CONGREGATIONAL UNION.

The annual meeting of the Liverpool section of the Lancashire Congregational Union was held on Tuesday afternoon at the Ashton-in•Makerfield Congregational Church. There was a large attend- ance of ministers and deacons. At the afternoon meeting Mr. W. Crosfield. M.P., presided.—The Rev. John Yonge, of Warrington,district secretary, intro- duced the business, giving a resume of last year's work at Orrell, near ‘Vigan.—Rev. J. A. Mitchell. 8.A., of St. Helens, then gave an address on finance, speaking of the various met hods of raising Church expenses, specially referring to pew rents, collec- tions, weekly offerings,and bazaars.—The discussion was continued by Revs. J. Riddette, G. Lord, J. Yonge, and Mr. 8; Eccles.—Before tea, Rev. H. Wilson invited ministers and delegates to go through the schools recently built by Miss Ruth Evans. The evening meeting was open to the pub- lic, and was presided over by Mr. Shorrock Eccles, of Huyton. It was well attended. Addresses were delivered by the Rev. A. W. Carter, of Huyton, on "-Congregationalism as a Formative Force in Character " ; the Rev. E. R. Barrett, 8.A., of Liver- pool, on "The Reunion of Vie Churches, but not via Grindelwald," and by the Rev. J. H. Riddette, of Havdock, on "Our Heritage."

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CONTRIBUTOR.

There seems to have been no end of jokes and fine points heard at some of our revision courts, but. Runcorn was entirely free from anything of such a nature. Throughout the whole of the proceedings there was nothing calling for special remark except perhaps the gracious compliment paid by the Re- vising Barrister to the Assistant Overseer (Mr. Sutton) and his colleague upon the perfect state ot the register. In effect, the barrister's words were, that in all courts which he had recently sat he had ' not had the pleasure of revising a more complete register and those responsible for the work of com- piling it had, very evidently, devoted considerable tiine and attention to it. He also referred in pleas- ing terms to the two political agents (Messrs. W. Handley and C. J. Hughes) without whose valuable assistance it would have been almost impossible for him to have finished the revision so soon. To hear such an exchange of courtesies is very agreeable to all concerned, and is an evidence of the good feel- ing existing between our registration authorities. In the course of my perigrinations this week I overhead a conversation the subject of which was the advisability of forming a Women's Liberal At- sociation so far as I could gather this matter is occupying the attention of our local Liberal worthies who will shortly hold a meeting among themselves to further discuss it. Such an organisa- tion appears to be very necessary and the wonder is that one has not been established before. Not only is the presence of the fair sex indispensable to the proper management of domestic affairs, but it almost equally needed in political affairs,women are fast becoming nearly inseparable from our public platforms ; every day they are coming more to the front; and every day we are realizing more and more how valuable their aid and counsel are in a multiplicity of things. The Local Government Act which will shortly be exercised will increase their importance in many directions, and will render such associations much more requisite. Our Liberal friends will therefore be acting wisely in constitut- ing a Women's Liberal Association as soon as possi- ble in order that Runcorn also may have the oppor- tunity of benefitting from the more direct influence of women upon its affairs.

Mr. J. T. Brunner, our popular Liberal Parliamen- tary member, is announced to open the St. John's Presbyterian Church Btizaar on Wednesday next, so that once again Runcornians will have the pleasure of listening to his voice. iie has fully recognised the worthiness of the object of the bazaar and,wirh his usual kindness has consented to come here and open the sale. It is to be hoped that a great many more folks will regard the event in the same light, and visit the schoolroom with the view of helping forward the scheme of the promoters, viz., to raise sufficient funds to justify them in proceeding with the erection of the church.

The Runcorn School Board, who have been so highly complimented upon the very successful way in which they have conducted the Science and Art Classes, and the Evening Continuation School, are re-opening these centres of instruction on October Ist. They have, as in past years, engaged the ser- vices of a qualified staff of teachers, and there is every reason to believe that quite as great, if not greater, success will be achieved in the future than in the past. The fees for both the Science and Art Classes, and Continuation School are so very reasonable as to be within the reach of t he poorest youth almost, and the advantages offered are exceptionally rare. To those youths whose desire it is to continue their studies after leaving the day school, these continuation classes must prove a blessing being superintended, as they are, by such a talented master and mistress. As in past years, the classes will meet in the Greenway-road Board Schools, where, on Monday evening, the prizes and certificates gained during the last session will be distributed to the successful scholars. It is earnest- ly hoped that the classes will be largely patronised, as they certainly deserve to be, and that the School Board will be thereby encouraged in the beneficial work in which they are at present engaged. 6

The Runcorn Technical Institute is every day approaching nearer to completion. To-day, it pre- sents, outside,a comparatively finished appeara;;ce, and strengthens the belief that in the course of a few months everything will be in readiness to carry on the work of the Science and Art classes. There is one thing that is rather bodeful, however, and that Is the dearth of subscriptions. It will severely handicap the committee if the Institute is not free from debt when opened, and it is, therefore, hoped that if there are any would-be subscribers to this most laudable undertaking, they will send in their gifts forthwith, in order to stimulate the committee an increase their funds.

div.head: P.S.A. AT IHE Y.M.C.A.
div.p: P.S.A. AT IHE Y.M.C.A.

On Sunday th- harvest festival was he!d at the - Y.M.C.A., Mr. Wm. Roberts oceupcing the chair. The address in the afternoon was given by Mr.W. Hickman. The musical portion of the service was undertaken by the Golborne-it. Baptist Chapel choir,who sang "Palms'', and "Ye shall dwell in the land" in an excellent manner. Mr. F. Hickman was the accompaniest. The Rev.D.W. Roberts and Mr. Flo'ford also took part in the meeting, which was the best attended and most successful that has vet been held. The room wis tastefully decorated with fruit, flowers, Svc.

div.head: ST. JAMES'.
div.p: ST. JAMES'.

The harveat festival in connection with St. James' Church was continned on Sunday. In the morning the Rev. Morley Stevensoq (Principal of the Warringtoa Training College) conducted the service at the choral celebration, and for his text he chose the words "Give iv; this day our daily bread." The Rev. F. Slater OS. c;ated in the evening. Appropriate hymns and an anthem were sung by the congregation, which was very large. This year's has been the brightest harvest festi- val held at St. James' for some time.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held at the above church on Thursday evening, and were conducted by the vicar (Rev. H. V. Pigot), and curates (Revs. J. E. Forbes and Townsend). The musical service consisted of Tours in F. and an anthem "The eyes of all wait upon thee," (Clare), appropriate hymns were also sung by the congregation. An excellent and appropriate sermon was preached by the Rev. G. H. St. Patrick Garrett, 8.D., (vicar of St. Paul's, Prince's Park. Liver- pool), on the text "For of him, and rhro' him, by him, and to him, are all things made; to him be glory." The interior of the building was very tastefully decorated with flowers, garlands, etc. A very large congregation was present and took an effective part in the singing. PADGATE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The weather on the occasion of the continuition of the annual harveA thanksgiving services at the Padgate Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday was very showery. The pulpit was occupied in the morning by the Rev. W. S. Hackett, of Didsbury, and in the evenine a very large congregation assembled to hear the Rev. J. S. Hughes, of Hill Cliff, who preached a very appropriate sermon. There was special music at each service, anthems being rendered by the choir, and a solo at the evening service by Miss Mary Bennett (Pear Tree House). Miss Jennie Bennett (Lyndhurst) was again at the organ. Collections were made at the close of each-service in aid of the circuit funds. After the evening service the de- corations were inspected by a large number of the con- gregation,who greatly admired them and remarked upon their artistic arrangements. ST. JOHN'S CHURCH, EARLESTOWN.

The annual thanksgiving services for the ingathering of the harvest were commenced in St. John's Church, Earlestown on Sunday. Much labour had been spent on the decoration of the interior of the church, and it ere- sented a very pleasing and seasonable appearance, fruit, flowers, vegetables and cereals being profusely arranged in various parts of the church. The pulpit was decorated by Miss Brotherhood, the font by Mrs. Mouncey, lectern, Mrs. G. Blair, and valuable assistance was rendered by Miss Appleton, Mr. Clough, the churchwardens and sidesmen. Large contributions of fruit, flowers and vegetables were sent by members of the congregation and friends. • At the morning and evening services on Sunday,t here were large congregations, especially in the evening, when the church was crlwded to excess, the pulpit being occupied by the Rev. P.R. A. Harpley,M.A., of Bolton, who delivered appropriate discourses At the morning service the choir sang the anthem "Ye shall dwell in the land," Miss Tripp taking the solo, and in the evening the anthem was " Behold how manifold." In the afternoon the Earlestown brass band was present, and after a short service played the following selections of inusie " Ora pro notis," " Star of Bethlehem," and " Great is the Lord." The band was also present at the evening service, and during the evening placed "The Holy City," "Rousseau's dream," and " The -Hallelujah Chorus." The services were continued on Monday even- mg when there was again a good congregation, the preacher being the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, M.A., vicar of Holy Trinity, Warrington. On Tuesday evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. T. J. Madden, vicar of St. Luke's, Liverpool.

div.head: WOTES FROM LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT.
div.p: WOTES FROM LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT.
(BY A LIMB Or THE LAW.)

The pollution of the River Mersey has been again to the front, and on Monday the Leigh and Tyides- ley Local Boards were each fined £2O and costs for allowing some of their impure sewage to go into the river. to my mind £2O and costs is a ridicul- ous small penalty for the offence. Every township on its banks should be fined at least £l,oooand then we should observe a real effort made in having the river as pure as possible. The banks of the river should be the favourite resort of the people both for residences and walks, but of course in its pre- sent condition the people keep away a" respectful distance." lam of course referring more particu- larly to the lower reaches of the river. Here in Liverpool we do get some pleasure from it. That the Mersey at Warrington was at one time in a satisfactory condition there is no doubt, and fish of various kinds were caught. Salmon were particu- larly abundant, and in the apprenticeship inden- tures the employers were compelled to covenant not to give their apprentices salmon more than twice a week. Imagine those times! But still there are plenty of fi,h in the river yet, and at, Egremont for the past few years I have seen hun- dreds of herrings caught; and if sewage and other poisonous matters were only kept out, there is no reason why herrings should not be caught at War- rington—as they would journey down with the tide, if the river was only made more comfortable for them.

The fruit costermongers who have been with us in Liverpool now for the last two seasons are again paying a visit to the stipendiary magistrate,but not of their own free will. It is no secret that not a few of the shopkeepers have been trying to teach the police their duty. The sympathy of the public is naturally with the " costers," because they have been the means of fruit being so much cheaper than formerly and it is also ready at hand. Castle- street is their favourite resort, and the offence is that they interfere with the traffic. So long as they keep moving and only stop to serve the customer they do not break the "law." Naturally, however, the "coster "gets tired of pushing his handcart along and he takes a long rest—too long a rest some of the shopkeepers consider and they want him out of the city. The coster however has come to stay; their numbers in spite of prosecutors are increasing.

We have been holding here,as is usual in all parts of the country a Revision Court, wherein both political parties endeavour to prevent each other from having any more votes placed on the register, if he or she (the voter) should not be of their political faith. The present condition of the fran- chise is disgraceful, and persons who are entitled to a vote will on a mere technicality or absurdity have their names struck off. It would simplify matters and certainly be more just if "age" was the only necessary qualification, commonly known as man- hood suffrage. Pie idea that property or residence should be a qualification is fast dying out. Writing about votes, reminds me. that Warrington has a Parliamentary representative—or is supposed to have one. lie appears to be one of those who does his work quietly. All the Warrington members have been of this class so far as I car. make out, with the exception of Mr. Peter Rylands and I imagine Warrington could do with such another for a change.

With regard to the Liverpool municipal elections next November a compromise has been adopted by both parties and it is arranged there is to be no con- test. Political organisation may arrange but it is possible that a few independent candidates may up- set this paper arrangement.

div.head: "WE'RE OETTIN' ON !"
div.p: "WE'RE OETTIN' ON !"

We're gettin' en ir Patricroft, Eaur streets are bein' paved ; An' thanks to diver Ceauncillors, 'Eaur rates 'ill aw be saved. Thay'rt hey ther due—the Dole gets his ! They're careful, to a rnon ; An' that's wot causes me to say, " We're gettm' on!" Behold Green Lone! theer yo con see nay boagle noan at price; An' its no wonder" Tommy " says, It makes his heart rtjice. Its Balm o' Gilead to his sow!, An' jv to that owd mon ; Wile o'er his "pipe an' glass" he owns " We're gettin' on !" Yon Band Stand, wi' its weather cock, In th' Recreation Greaund, Is summut we can brag abeaut— (But duz that cork turn reaund?) It makes uz feel eaur Ceauncillors Are doin' aw thay con To keep eaur RWes deawn, an' to show "We're gettin' on !" Fro th' Packet Heause an reaund abeaut, (Yole smell it as yo pass—) Thav'n made a hole I—it met be coal They're workin' for, not gas. God said, " let there be light," and so This skame thay'n hit upon; Another proof to th' nayburs reaund— "We're gettin' on I" An' neaw seen riz to th' dignity Ov a fost-rate Finger Post; That puts us reet fer th' Ship Cane!!, An' aw th surreaundin' Coast! So If a stranger gets lost neaw, It shows his wits hez gone; An' whether he guz wrung er not, "We're gettin' on !" But wheel; west lick aw th' country reaund, Is hevin' chaps to grow The grandest dahlias an' chrysanti, Per bestin' anny show! Aw sizes, fro' a penny piece, To a farm-heause fryin' poll; Which tells eaur Council Wry day, "We're gettin' on !" One chap aw know—a chum o' raine— He raises um i' beds; Sum on urn wi' a big fleawer grown, An' sum on um beaut yeds! Sum wi' white fleet caps reaund, just like A lately sentenced mon, That's bin fixed fer his last lung drop— " He's gettin' on !" Eaur Ceauncillors encourage this, At least so aw've bin towd, Fer coaxin' th' Church to th' Noss'ry Greaund, An' gettin' th' floaw'rs wee! sowd. Its just th' time, too, when pious folk Ther churches like to don Wi' nice green grocery, to show Thay're gettin' on !" Is ther owt else? Well, aw think not, Aw think aw've sed enuff To show yo that eaur Ceauncillors Are chaps that's "up to snuff !" Th' Election time 'ill soon be here, Wen we mun choose eaur mon ; An'—secked er not—aw'm sure he'll say, "We're gettin' on !" TUM 0' PEGS. Rose Bonk, Septembor 28, 1894.

div.head: SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT AND, WELSH
div.p: SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT AND, WELSH
DESCENT.

The" Brecon and Radnor Express" of September 21, in a query signed "The Editor," says :—" I hear it con- fidently asserted that the present Chancellor of the Exchequer (Sir William Harcourt) is descended from a Welsh family—in fact, a Breconshire family. From Jones's Breconshire,' vol. 111., pp. 484-490, it will be found that in the year 1705, Godfrey Harcourt, of Dan- y-Parc, was High Sheriff of Breconshire; he married a daughter of Richard Lewis, of Dan-y-Parc. In 1730, Lewis Harcourt, Godfrey's son, was high sherriff. In 1747, Charles Harcourt, of Dan-y-Parc, was high sheriff. Charles had a son Richard, who died at the early age of twenty-four, on May 18,, 1723; and another son, John ' Harcourt, who also was high sheriff in 1754 ; John Har- court left an only daughter, Letitia, who was the second wife of Henry Skrine. This Henry Skrine lived at Dao- y-Parc, and by Miss Harcourt he had a family of seven children. He died in 1803. His widow sold Dan-y-Parc to Mr. Edward Kendal, who started the ironworks at Beaufort. Now we get these broad facts that in 1650- 1700 Godfrey Harcourt settled in Breconshire as agent for the Somerset family, and married the heiress of Lewis, of Dan-y-Parc. Two of.the Harcourt daughters married Williams, oi Llangattock Court, and Powell of Peterstone. The Harcourt that came to Breconshire was beyond a doubt one of the Stanton Harcourts and Nune- ham Hareourts, Sir William Harcourt's son bears the name of Lewis. Thi.s leads to the following queries :- 1. Has Sir William Harcourt any Welsh blood in his veins? 2. Are there any descendants of the Harcourt family in Breconshira now on the female side?

div.head: HOW TO ELEC r THE DISTRICT COUNCIL
div.p: HOW TO ELEC r THE DISTRICT COUNCIL

Last week we published a synopsis of the rules for the election of parish councillors. A General Order has now been issued giving the rules as to the nomination and election of Rural District Coun- cillors. Copies have been sent to the County Coun- cil of every administrative county in England and Wales (except the County of London), the Board of Guardians of every Poor Law Union in England and Wales, which on "the appointed day" will be coextensive with or will contain a rural parish, and to the overseers of every rur. I parish. THE ACT. To begin with, certain sectons of the Local Government Act, 1894, are explained, and from these (Sections 20-24) the re'ations of the boards of guardians and the rural district councils are made clear. In the first place it is stated that the person to be elected must be a parochial elector, and that no person is disqualified by sex or marriage. In Section 21 it is enacted that : " For every rural sanitary district there shall be a rural district coun- cil, whose district shall be called s rural district," and in section 24:

The number of councillors for each parish or other area in a rural district shall be the same as the number of guardians for that parish or area. The district councillors for any parish or other area in a rural district shall be the representatives of that parish or area on the board of guardians,and when acting in that capacity shall be deemed to be guardians of the poor, and guardians as such shall not be electedlor that parish or area. In Section 48 it is provided that the poll shall be taken by ballot—an improvement in the election of guardians which will be heartily welcomed when it comes into operation. "THE APPOINTED DAY."

After stating that the eturning Officer for the rural council elections shall be the clerk to the guardians, or, in his absence, a person appointed by the guardians the general order announces :--• The day of the election of rural district coun- cillors• in the parish in the year 1894 shall be Mon- day, Dec. 17, in that year, or such other day, not being earlier than Saturday, Dec. 15th, of later than Wednesday, the 19 h, as may for special reasons, be fixed by the county council. Provided that the day of election of rural district councßiore in the parieh and the day of the poll for the election of any parish councillors to be elected at the same date in the parish shall be the same. Notice of the election mu-t be prepared not later than Dec. I', and posted about the parishes in the district.

div.head: NOMINATION.
div.p: THE NOMINATION.

Each candidate is to be nominated in writing,one name in each nomination paper, the description of the candidate being accompanied by the name of the parish or area for which he is put forward. There is also the important prlviso that a parochial elector shall not sign more papers than there are f.b.ouncillors to be elected; and, further, that he shall not sign for a parish or other area in which he is not registered as a parochial elector. The nomina- tion forms will be obtainable from the returning officer or overseers free of charge. The papers must be handed in at the returning officer's office not later than two o'clock on December sth. No later than December ith the officer shall publish a state- ment of the nominations received, indicating whether they are valid or not. THE ELECTION.

If the number of valid nominations exceeds that of persons to be elected, the councillors shall be elected from the persons nominated; if the num- ber is the same the returning officer shall on December 7th give notice to each candidate who has not with irawn stating that he has been chosen. Public notice is to be given when a poll is found to be not necessary. The poll, if any, shall be on the date given above (see " Appointed Day") between the hours fixed by the county council, so, however, that the poll shall always be open between six and eight o'clock in the evening. As to polling districts the following provision is macie : If the parish is divided into polling districts for the election of county councillors or of parish coun- cillors, the whole of each such district being com- pri.ed in the parish, and the lists of parochial elec- tors are made out in separate parts for such dis- tricts, each district shall be a polling district for the election of rural district councillors.

If the parish is divided into wards for the elec- tion of parish councillors the same may be utilised for district councillors. But if neither of the above conditions exit the returning officer may divide the parish, but each district, must cover an area for which separate lists of parochial electors are avail- able. _ _

div.head: POLL.
div.p: THE POLL.

The number and situation of the polling stations shall be fix.d by the returning officer, under cer- tain wise restrictions. No premises licensed for the sale of intoxicating liquor shall be utilised, and the same stations shall be used for the election of dis- trict. and parish councillors. Five clear days' notice shall be given when a poll has to be taken, giving full descriptions and particulars of the num- ber to be elected, the persons nominated, with the proposers and seconders,the situation of the polling places,and the hours fixed for voting. One notice may be given to cover the el.ctions of both rural and dis- trict councillors. The returning officer and persons nominated by him (chosen from the pirish where po.sible) shall act as presiding officers at each poll- ing station. Polling agents to represent candidates are allowed under certain regulations. There are further clauses for the counting of the votes and the declaration of the poll, which shall be made by the returning officer, who shall "forthwith cause a copy of it to be affixed io the front of the building in which the votes have been counted."

div.head: IN FFICE.
div.p: IN FFICE.

The rural district councillors elected shall come into office on Dc. 28. It is further ordered : If the rural district is situate in more than one Poor Law Union, the returning officer, for the pur- pose of convening the first meeting of the Rural Di-trict Council, shall be the retnrning officer at the election of rural district councillors in that part of the district which, according to the census of 1891, has the larger population. The expenses of the election come upon the parishes and wards concerned. A number of sche- dules and forms of papers to be used are issued with the General Order.

div.head: ST. HELENS CORPORATION WATER ESTATE.
div.p: ST. HELENS CORPORATION WATER ESTATE.
THE REPAYMENT OF OLD LOANS.

At the monthly meeting of the Finance Committee of the se. Helens Corporotion, on Wednesday, Alderman J. C. Gamble presiding, the Borough treasurer (Mr. John Brown)reported that last week he paid off the remaining loan authorised under the Acts of 1851 and 1855 on General and Waterworks Accounts. When the St. Helens Commissioners purchased the undertaking of the old St. Helens Water Company the only source of supply was the dams at Eccleston, and the yield was quite in- adequate for the wants of a growing population. The Ants above mentioned were obtained, and a sum of £25.000 was borrowed. With this freehold land was purchased at Eccleston Hill. wells wle sunk, engine- houses erected, and mains laid to supply the district. Under the 1851 Art the loan was repayable in thirty years, and under the 1855 Act the loan was repayable in forty years. It is interesting to not that when the money WRS borrowed the rate of interest was 5 per cent., but as small loans expired they were renewed at the rates of 41. 44, 4. 3-t 34, 34, and lastly at. 3 per cent. The announcement that the loan of £25.000 had all been paid was practically a statement that the valuable pumping station at Encleston Hill had become the absolute pro- perty of the Corporation. The information was received with much satisfaction by the committee, and on the motion of the Mayor (Alderman Sinclair), seconded by Mr. Joseph Massey,the fact was ordered to be entered on the minutes.

div.head: ST. HELENS HEALTEI COMMITTEE.
div.p: ST. HELENS HEALTEI COMMITTEE.
THE SMOKE NUISANCE.

- --- - At the St. Helens Health Committee, cn Wednesday afternoon, Mr. John Forster presiding, a letter was read from the Clerk to the County Councii, calling attention to the powers conferred upon them to deal with smoke, and pointing out that smoke from mills and works in the county boroughs Was a source of nuisance to resi- dents in the administrative county. The Chairman thought it would be better if more smoke was knocking about St. Helens. (Hear, hear.) No action was decided upon. The Borough Surikeyor reported on the question of sewering from Windle City to Denton's Green, in the area of the borough extension. The Local Government Board had sanctioned the borrowing of £2,0.00 for the work, and the orginal scheme was for earthenware pipes. The question had been raised whether brick should not be substituted for earthen- ware. The Surveyor said nine-inch brickwork would be a very serious item, and cost more money, but if they put in four and a half inch work there would only be an extra expenditure of about £l5O in the excavations. He thought four and a half inch work would he suffi- dent, and Major-General Hutchinson, of the Board of ' Trade, agreed with him.—Councillor Fisher, a local builder, said that a four and a half inch sewer was quite sufficient if it was done in cement.—lt was decided to carry out the scheme with four and a half inch brick- work, and advertise for tenders.
NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
BY A.N OCCASIONAL CORIIESPONDRNT.

This is a great place for teetotallers, and accord- ing to all accounts, our local tenap.-rance orgauisa- tions are adding greatly to their membership. This especially refers to the Good Templar lodges, one of which has increased by leaps aud hounds, until it has become a matter of serious consideration, whether a more commodious meeting reum will not- have to be engaged.

The Viaduct Institute Technical Instruction classes are now in full swing, and the number of students enrolled in the various science and art subjects is so far very satisfactory. Stieb,however, cannot be said of the domestic classes,.whicii have been instituted for the education of the ladies in household management. Perhaps in the suhjeets of cookery and laundry the committee do not. grumble, but in that of "making and mending garments," the response to the invitation of the committee for the formation of classed has not by any means been generous. Now hereie I think our modern house- wives, and those who entertain th-ughts of at one time becoming wives, make a serious mistake. Blys and girls are naturally rough, if healthy, and they do not pay any great respect to the stability ot their garments, and the consequence often is an alarming rip or tear in their breeches or frocks. Now, if a woman is not handy with her needle,this rip or tear is pulled together in a slovenly manner, and presents an ugly appearance, but if she has received a course of instruction in the art of mak- ing and mending garments, she would be able to repair the rent in sueh a tnann,Jr that its presence could not he detected. This branch of industry has become quite a fine art on the Continent, and the presence of ragged tar unzidy children is quite a . rarity. and I think it would be well if a few more of our workingmen's wives followed the example. They have every opportunity at the Institute classes,and the fee would be motley well spent.

There is also another branch in the domestic classes which is not, receiving the at ten fiNn ir ought to do' and that is "Sick nursing." Now I don't think anyone will deny the importance of this branch °rawly, for its benefits in a household are manifold. Where there is a large family, the value of a knowledge of sick nursing at home, cannot be over estimated. At the In-titute it is propo-ied to ' give a course of 10 lectures on the sutlect,providing a sufficient number of students be eurol.ed. So far, however, only a very •mall number have given in - their names, and of coursa the c.-mmtnittee do not feel warranted in engaging teac,lers, to conduct such a class at a loss. in the lectures whin') it is proposed to give, are included" dealtli and how to preserve it," " The sick ro )m," "Children's ail- ments,"" Accidents," &c, an I from this it wlll be ' seen how invaluable a knowledge of these things must be to woman with a family. Anyone wishing to join for either of these subj•-cts, can do so by applying to Mr. Galloway, at 192, Crow-lane.

The meeting last week in connection with tha District Council Question turned out as I antici- pated, in fact I do not see what else could be done. Yet, beyond arriving at some understanding in re- gard to the candidates to be re-elected, 1 do not see what practical good will result.—The tact of ward committees being appointed to make selections, does not prevent any two independent ratepfiyers nominating another outside the CnnunittePs selec- tion, as a candidate for the honour of Councillor. And in order to put a stumbling block in the way of any would-be aspirant, the only thing the Com- mittee will hive to do will be when they have de- cided on candidates to call the ratepayers in the respective wards together, and get their opinion, and a pledge that they will stand by the Committee on the eventful day, and vote only for their selec- tions.—From what I can hear there is likely to be some scrambling for places, and in that Case there will consequently be some hard fighting and cross voting.

Mr. Stewart, relieving officer, stated that the prisoner disappeared on the tth August, and his wife had since been main- tained by the Union at eest of £2 ss. The prisoner was sent to prison for 14 days. ASSMILTING A Sr. HELENS FOREMAN. AtSt.. Helens Police Court on Monday, Patrick Doran < and Patrick Kelly. of 24. It appeared that in consequence of a complaint by Cook a man named Farrell was discharger-I from his work. Cook. was met on Sundar afternoon, while he was going to work, by Doran and Kelly, anti they,acc.)rdine to Cook's story, savagely attacked him, Doran remarking that he would not get another man “sacked." P. was admitted that Doran while drunk had assaulted Cook, but Mr. Riley contended tha' Kelly had nothing to do with it.— - They were each fined 204. and costs or a month. THE MONICIP(L ELECTIONS. . div.head: SAILOR'S FREAK.
div.p: A SAILOR'S FREAK.

A Crewe correspondent sends a remarkable story of railway journeying. Be says that as the Bristol express was running out of Crewe station on Thursday a sailor sprang on the bliff:.r of the last carriage. Away sped the train with the seaman carelessly mit ride the peril- ous seat. At Frees the guard,accri tinted by telegraph of the passenger's freak, urged the m .n to miter a compart- ment, but the sailor was reluctant to ga t his novel posi- tion, and sail. "Go on; I'm all right." F nally he was induced to get into a carriage and continue his journey in the ordinary way.

div.head: STREET RIoT AT WIDNES. WOMEN RESCUING PRI ;ONERS FROM THE POLICE.
div.p: A STREET RIoT AT WIDNES. WOMEN RESCUING PRI ;ONERS FROM THE POLICE.

On Thursday, at the Widues Petty Sessions. before Messrs. E. K. Muspratt and J. C. Gamble, John Lynch, 13, Edmnnd-street,was summoned for ereating a breach of the peace in Edmund-street on the 22.1 d in t.; Patrick Cain, his mother, Bridget Cain, Margaret Lynch, Johanna Lynch, and Cotherine Lynch, all re4idlng In Edmund-street, were summon( /1 for assaulting Police.. constable Bamforth on the same night; and Lynch mad the other five persons were further charged wttn assault- ing Police-constable Hamilton at the same time and place. Bridget Cain and the three women Lynch were also charged with doing wilful damage to the uniform of Police-constable Hamilton. Superintendent Keightey said all the cases arose out ot the case of breach of the peace against Lynch. It appears that at 10.15 on Saturday night the two constables, Bamforth and Hamilton saw the man Lynch in Ann-street creating a disturbance. They requested him to desist, and a young man took him home. Later on the same night (about five minutes to twelve) the constables found Lynch in Victoria-street quarrelling with a man. Hamil- ton went up to Lynch, who struck tht: fficer twice on the side of the head and knocked his helmet off The.... defendant Cain then got hold of Hamilton by the legs and lift d him up. The women then came up and took the two men Lynch and Cain from the custody of the ' constables, and tore the tunic and trou-ers of Constable Hamilton. Bamferth was also badly assaulted, and if ' the bench thought after they had heard the evidence that ' the case w is proved, he (Superintendent Keighley) asked them to deal out such puniAment to these pers( na as would be a warning to other people. These assaults on the police were becoming much too frequent in Widnes —The two officers corroborated this statement. They said there was a very large crewd of people in the street, and they were both very roughly handled. It was the action of the four women which caused the two men to escape from their custody.—The defendants all accused Constable Hamilton of being drunk and being the cause of the disturbance, but Inspector Mricaland and Police- sergeants Thwaites and Radcliffe were called and denied that Hamilton was under the influence of drink.—The- bench thought there was a doubt in the case of Johanna Lynch, and discharged her.—Previous convictions were- recorded against John Lynch and the two Cain s T,vtich was sent to gaol for one month with hard lab, e :and Patrick Cain for a similar term ; the tl;r( e wow, were. each fined 255. including costs, with the alternate of fourteen days' imprisonment.

div.head: VALUABLE DISCOVERY.
div.p: A VALUABLE DISCOVERY.

Most readers have had some experience of sick rooms, either as patients or attendants. How many such are there who have not felt the weakness or debility which follows the sickness, more discouraoing_, than even the disease itself? Though the disease may have given way before the timely application of proper remedies, and though, in consequence, no immediate danger is to be apprehended, the slow progress towards convalescence is very disheartening to patient and attendant alike.

How often do we hear people say :—" Yes. The fever has left him. He is free from any immediate danger. But he is so weak. If he could only regain strength !" This debilitating effect of fevers and other diseases is indeed a great source of anxiety to medical men as well as to their patients ; and anything which would tend directly to shorten the period between the departure of the fever and the complete recovery of strength would be naturally welcomed by both doctors and patients.

This is one of the reasons why Gwylyrn Evans' Quinine Bitters are so popular,why doctors prescribe it so largely, why chemists sell it so generally, why patients have recourse to it so readily, and why everybody has a good word to say for it. Not only does it attack the disease in its stronghold, not only does it drive the evil from the system, but it gives bark directly the strength of which the system has been deprived by sickness ; it infuses new life into the blood, and the recovery of health sad strength, instead of being, as it otherwise would be, discouragingly slow, intermittent, and uncer- tain, becomes, when this excellent medicine is resorted to, encouragingly rapid, regular, and certain. It is, therefore, confidently recommended as an unrivalled tonic medicine,and may be safely used by all who suffer from any form of weakness or debility from whatever cause it may arise.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THE ASSAULT WITH A GUN_ BARREL.

A youth named Wm. Dobson. of Moore, was charged on remand at Daresbury Petty Sessions en ruesday,with having on the 257 h August at Moore assaulted George White. The aharge had been reduced from one of un- lawful wounding. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, represented the defendant. The case against Dobson was that on the night of the date named, after receiving a thrashing from White on the canal bank at Moore, he struck him a severe blow with a gun barrel. White was stunned with the blow and was taken home by a companion named Banner. He was under medical treatment for the injuries he received for some time. Dobson at the time was also in possession of a carving knife but this was taken from him and thrown into the canal. Evi- dence for the prosecution was given by George White, James Banner, and P.C. Shatwell. Mr. Jenkins, for the defence, stated that White was the aggressor, he having knocked Dobson to the ground in the first instance. After Such provocation it was no wonder that he retaliated in the way he did. It was a school boy's fight and nothing would have been heard of the matter had not the gun barrel been brought into Use. The magis'rates 'sound the defendant over to keep the peace for six months, and ordered him to pay the costs, £1 N. 6d. in all.

div.head: THEFT OF SLATES.
div.p: THEFT OF SLATES.

At the Borough Police Court, on Saturday, John Titchett was charged with stealing from a building in Winmarleigh-st., at half-past six on Friday evening, a quantity of slates value 35., the property of Charles W. Davenport, builder and contractor, residing at Stockton Beath.—Mr. Hunt (chief constable) said that the de- fendant was a jobbing slater by trade, residing in corn- -mon lodging-houses.—D.S. Monaghan stated that at half-past six on the day in question he was in Sankey- St. near the Town Hall gates when he saw the prisoner coming up Winmarleigh-st. with something bulky under his arm. On the prisoner catmhing sight of witne,s Le attempted to get away unobserved, but Monaghan stopped him and wked him where he got the slates, and the prisoner replied that he got theca from Bank Quay. Be afterwards confessed that he had stolen the slaters from some buildings in ccurse of erection in Winmar- leigh-st. Monaghan brought the prisoner to the police station and locked him np.--Mr. Samuel Dallam stated that he came to represent Mr. Davenport. Daring the Last few weeks a number of building Riaterials had been stolen. Therefore he wished to press the case against the prisoner.—The magistrates sent the prisoner to gaol for one month's hard labour.
CHARGE OF KEEPING DANGEROUS DOGS.

At Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Richard Robinson, Lower Stretton, and James Highfieid, Lower Stretton, were charged with having on the I,t S-pt. been the owners of dangerous dogs, and with not having kept them under proper control. Mr A. Browne, solicitor, represented the defendant, Robinson.—John Ellison stated that or. the 31st August, at du k, he was passing the defendant Robinson's house when he heard the stamp of a foot and on looking round, saw Robinson in a stoop-, ing position. Three dogs immediately set upon witness, and he was fighting with the dogs for about four minutes. One dog was at the hack of him, and two others at the front. Robinson who was standing at his door saw what was occurring but did not for some time call the dogs away. The dogs left him when Robinson called. Witness was badly bitten, and had to go to a doctor to have the wounds dressed. On going to Robin- son's house to see about the matter, the dorr was Slammed in his face. P.C. Bratt stated that about twelve months ago he received a complaint from a man named Fitzgerald who told him that he had been bitten by a dog belonging to Robinson, who owned two large fox terriers. The other dog which set upon the complainant was a spaniel and belonged to the defendant Eighfield. Witness cautioned Robinson twelve months ago. He saw Ellison's wounds which were on the hack and front of the legs. Blood had been drawn. Mr. Browne stated that his client was very sorry that these dogs had bitten Mr. Ellison. But they did not know a man had been bitten until the police came with a summons. Mr. Robinson absolutely denied that he had ever heard any complaints as to his dogs biting anyone. They were kept as pets, and were not ferocious. He asked the magistrates not to destroy the dogs. Evidence was given by several neighbours to show that the dogs were not ferocious, but pets and that children played with them. The magistrates ordered the defendants to pay the costs and warned them that the dogs must be kept under proper control. The Chairman (Mr. Long) remarked that on the Ist October an order was te, be issued by the County Council for all dogs to be muzzled, in conse- quence of rabies in the county. Inspector Plan- stated that the defendant had two stalls in the Market. A space was marked out showing stallholders where they could put their hampers. The defendant overstepped the mark three feet. She hid been cautioned several times before.—The magistrates tined her 54. including costs. The defendant had done so, and he (Mr. Shearer wished to withdraw the case.—The magistrates con- curred, and the defendant was discharged. A NEGLECTFUL BORROWER.—WiIIiam Williams was charged with stealing by means of a trick from Henry Wilson, on Sunday, the 16'.h inst., a riding saddle, value 203., his property.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty.—From the statement of the Chief ConFtable it appeared that the prisoner, who is a groom, went to Mr. Wilson on the date named and 4ated that Mr. K-ndrick, of the Lion Hotel, wished to borrow a riding saddle for about ten minutes in order to try a cob. Mr. Kendrick, however, kri:!vv nothing about the saddle, and had not authorivat anyone to birrow one. The police were informed and D.S. Mon Ighan found the prisoner drinking in the Bridge-st. vaults. It was ascertained that he had been using the saddle on one of Mr. Spann's horses, of Friars-green, but Mr. S3anri knew nothing If the borrowing of the saddle. It was found on Mr. Spann's premises.—Evidence supporting Mr. Hunt's o.atement was given by Messrs. W. Wilson, W. C are, Kendrick, and D S. Monaghan —The prisoner admitted borrowing the saddle in Mr. Kendrick's name, but said he intended to return it, and had no idea of stealing it. The magistrates sail they could scarcely call it theft,and discharged him.

div.head: OCCASIONAL COURT. SATURDAY.—More Mr. John White,
div.p: OCCASIONAL COURT. SATURDAY.—More Mr. John White,

DAMAGING TURNIPS —Arthur Stevonson and William S irsfield were charged with doing wilful damage to a (plan ity of turnips in a field belonging to N. Fowles. Woolston, on September 22nd .—Sergt. Barnes in proving the case, said the police had received numerous com- plaints about this class of off.mce, and not,ces had been posted in the district calling attention to it.—Prisoners were each flied 53. and costs, or seven days' imprison- ment in default. ALLEGED THEFT.—George Caulson was charged with stealing a quantity of waste, value is. 10d., the property of John Jackson, from a store-house at Arpley, nia the 21. t of September. The prisoner was remanded to the Wa.rrinton Petty Sessions. MONDAY. —Befrr- Mr. S. R. Armitage. . .

VAGRANCY.—AIPxand,,r Unsworth was charged with slPeping in a barn at Rixton, and having no apparent moans of subqistence.—P.C. Ryder proved the case.— Prisoner for similar offences has been before the magis- trates eight times and sent to gaol for 14 days.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Long (chairman), Alderman H. Niel& and the Hon. Harvey Talbot. DAMAGING TELEGRAPH INSULATORS.—WaIter Fryer, 13 years of age, residing with his parents at 109, Sharpe- st., Warrington, was charged with having en the 29th July, damaged certain wires and insulators belonging to H.M. Government, by throwing stones. Mr. Gorton, employed at the Warrington Post Office, stated that he appeared on behalf of the Postmaster-General.—P.C. Brett deposed that in the company with Sergeant Gosling on the date named he was near the stone quarry at Appleton when he a,ve four boys throwing stones. The defendant was the only one that threw et the telegraph wires. The Inspector of telegraphs in the district stated that in the district mentioned there had been 57 insula- tors broken. The cost averaged about one shilling each. —Mr. Gorton said the post office authorities did not wish to press the case against the defendant. A small fine and the costs would be sufficient.—The magistrates imposed a fine of 2s. 61. and costs, 17s. in all. A WARRINGTON BAKER FlNED.—James Hallwood, baker, Wdderspool Causeway, was charged with having on the 14th S litember at Daresbury, had in use for trade, a weighing instrument enstamped. Defendant pleaded guilty. —Mr. Wm. Dunlop Laird, inspector of weights and measures, stated that he saw a servant of defendent's delivering bread from a van at Daresbury on the date named. He asked for the production of the scales when he had handed to him the spring balance , produced. It was utastamped, and was also two ozs. light in four lbs.—The defendant stated that the spring balance was supplied to him by the post office authori- ties for weighing their parcels at his shop, which was used as a branch post office. He sent it out in the bread van because there was no room in the van for a pair of scales —He was tined 5. arid costs. AN EXTRAORDINARY INCIDENT.—AIfred Groves, 48, Lowe-st., Sr. Helens, was charged with having on the 22nd July at Walton, committed a trespass by being on land in the possession of Mr. John Weir in search of game. Defendant pleaded not guiltv.—Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, stated that the magistrates would remember that at the last court he appeared to prosecute a man named smith on a similar charge to the present one. The defendant Smith called a witness who gave his name ac Alfred Groves and, swore that Smith was at St. Helens at the time of the alleged offence. The man Groves was identifiPd by John Irlarfn game- keeper, as the man who was in company with 'Smith in search of aame, and a summons had been taken out against him. He (Mr Browne) did not think that the man who now enswered the summons was the same as gave evidence on behelf of Smith.—Mr. Irlam, game- keeper, stated that he could not recognise the defendant. He did not look like the man that gave evidence on the last occasion. He believed that the man in the box was brother to the man that gave evidence on the last. occa- sion, whom he (witness) identified.—The defendant statpd that he was at that court on the last occasion,and that he was Alfred Groves.—Mr. Browne stated that he could not receenise the man, and he did not think he was the witness that, eave the name of Alfred Groves It was a most extranelinary case.—The Chairman stated that if they could not identify the man the Bench could do nothing hut di.eniesi the Case. SCHOOL ATTENDINCE CA.ES.—Mr. Jenkins, school at- telidanee offieer, prosecuted, in the following cases of irregular attendanre at school :—.Joseph Gerrard, Water- worlzs. Appleton, twe children ; Spptimus Travis,Stock- ton Heath, fined 2s. 6d.

CRUELTY To A Honsm.—John Pover, farmer, of Dun- ham Hill, was charged with causing a horse to be ill- treated on the 6th Angust, at Iltine,orn, by allowing the same to be worked when in an unfit state.—Defendant s denied the charae.—P C. Buller gave evidence, saving that when he saw the animal, it, was attached to a light spring cart, and wa in a very lame condition, suffering from a sT.Yollen fetlociz.—insneor Hicks spoke to seeing the animal at the Vine Hotel. Lowlands-road, where it had been lodged in obedience to the last officer's instructions. When the defendant was questioned with regard to the horse's state, he answered that a fortnight; since the animal had run a nail into its hoof in Church- street and that the wound had been properly attended to. WO. Tipp,c w that. the fptloc.k was much swollen, and that tallow had been placed inside the wound.— TM:Meet-or Luff, of the R.S P.C.A. also gave testimony, after which the defendant, in addressing the Bench ,said the mare was all right when she was turned out on the morning of the day named. A fortnight before the hcrse was stormed by the first witness, it had run a nail into its foot in Church-street, Runcorn. and the wound had been attended to by the unfortunate blacksmith who had, a few days ago,cemmitted snicide at Runcorn. Ho cared evi,len,e to the effect that the horse, when on ire way to Runcorn, began to kpck, and said that most hkely the wound was thPrehy irritated.—Defendant was fined ICh, and 12' 61. coats or fon-teen &kr, in t7aol. Tne house was not fit to live in, beeause in one of the rooms there was a large hole in the eeiling ene his chil- dren were made ill thereby.—Ellen Done deposed to see- ing the defendant remove his goods in the forenoom of the 3rd September. She saw none removed at night.— In answer to the magistrates,defenda,nt said he supposed the house, where he now lived would be registered in his name as the tenant. He had net as yet, however, seen the rent book so could not tell.—The prosecutor a4mitted that the defendant had told him that he would move out before the arrears were paid and he (prosecu- tor) then told him that he must not.—The Chairman thought that the prosecutor and defendant had better come to some arrangement about the payment of the arrears. There did not appear to be any evidence of fraudulent removal in the case. The defendant had said that he would move, and the prosecutor ought not to keep a tenant boxed up in a houce because he could not pay the heavy demand made of him.—The agent interrupted by saying that the man had occupied the house for ten years.—The Chairman answered that if that was the case the agent should have given him a little mere consideration. The case would be dismissed. The defendant as he left the court, said to the Bench that he had very good reasons for le lying the house. DRUNKENNESS.—Stephen Perrin was fined ss.including costs for being drunk on the 15 h September in Weston- road.—Lawrence Burke, hailing from Wrexham, and who said that he was employed at Widnes, was fined ss. including costs for being drunk and disorderly on the 22nd September in Mersey-street. A YOUTHFUL PICKPOCKET.—Thomas Stanton, aged 18 years, was charged in euatody with being a suspected person and with frequenting the Runcorn Market Place OR the previous Baturclay night with intent to commit a felony.—Constables Gregory and Richardson stated that at about nine o'clock on the previous Saturday night they were on duty outside the Market Place, where a vendor of goods had drawn together a crowd, when they saw the prisoner put his hand into a lady's pocket. He turned round and when he saw the officers he bolted but was very SO m afterwards caught. The prisoner, who denied this statement, was committed to prison for four- -teen days with hard labour.

FRODSHAM PET FY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY. —Befoie Messrs. C. Reynolds, and T. Rigby. JURY LIST. —Mr. Astle, jun., assistantoverseer for the township of D4rnhill present id a list of p-rsons qualified to serve on juries.—The Chairman informed him that by not taking the list to 041rmere Petty Sessions he had subjected himself to a severe reprimand and a penalty of -210.—The assistant,overseer replied that the notifica- tion of the sessions was thrown into his house by a policeman and had been mislaid.—P.S. Hunt remarked that such a proceeding was very irregular, as the con- stabulary were not allowed to deliver notices in such a manner.

TEMPORARY AUTHORITY.—The magistrates granted Mary Elam, of Five rirosses, temporary authority to sell at a beerhouse, the license of which had been held by her late husband. BREACH or THE Byx-Lews.—William Walker, Hus- kinson-street, Liverpool, was summoned on tne com- plaint of James Farrington, nuisance inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, for occupying two dwelling houses, 70 and 72 Main-street, Frodsham with- out having a certificate showing that there was a plenti- ful supply of wholesome water.—The evidence showed that the defendant had applied fora certificate since the proceedißgs were commenced. There was a supply of water.—Mr. Samuel Davies, representing the defendant, said that the matter was one of pure inadvertence on the part of Mr. Walker.—Fined 61. and costs in each case.
NON-PAYMENT OF RATES.—Several persons were Sum- moned for not paying their rates, and in the unsettled cases the Bench made orders for payment within a week.

THE EDUCATION ACT.—For not sending his child regu- larly to school, Samuel Yowl, Booth-st, Frodsham, was find 53. including costs. EMPLOYER AND EMPLOYEE.—Wm. Henry W. Frankish (a boy) summoned his employer, Henry Gilbert,Watson- st., Frodsham Lordship,for having assaulted him on the 10th September. The complainant stated that the quarrel arose because he would not accept his wages yearly in- stead of weekly. He had been struck and kicked by defendant. This was denied by the defendant,who said that the boy was abusing some pigs and he (defendant) put him out of the sit:A.—Dismissed. A DRU,KEN DRIVER. For being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap on August 26th at Frodsham, Thomas Brigand, M tin-st., was fined 53. and costs.— Dofendarit admitted the offence. UNMUZZED AND UNCOLLARED. Owen Frodsham, of Newton, was fined 6.1. 83. 6J. costs for allowing his dog to stray minus the necessary muzzle and collar on the 15th September. A NOISY TIPSTER.—SamueI Spruce, Frodsham Lord- ship, wa3 fined 53. including costs for being guilty of riotous conduct whilst drunk at Frodsham Lordship on the 2nd September. DISGRACEFUL BEHAVIOUR ON A SUNDAY NIGHT.—Thos. C,rter, Frodsham Lordzhip, was summoned for coin. mitting a breach of the peace by fighting at Frodsham on the 2nd September.—Sergeant Hunt testified that on the night of the above date three sailors came to him and said that they were afraid of going to Saltport be- cause some men were .lying in wait for them. He in- structed them to go on and he would follow. After going some distance they were pounced upon, and when the officer arrived defendant and another man were on the ground. This sort of conduct was common in the locality. The defendant, when questioned, gave the name of Thos. Williams, Bradley.—Defendant, who ad- mitted the offence wag bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months and was ordered to pay the costs, 103. 6d.
