div.head: WARRINGTON y. ROCEIDALE HORNETS.
div.p: WARRINGTON y. ROCEIDALE HORNETS.

These teams played off their first fixture at the Wilders- pool enclosure on Saturday. Neither side had a very brilliant record up to date, but a vi s t )ry ior Warrington was generally expected. Last year's matches between the combatants were of a satisfactory character to War- rington, who were successful in each encounter, al- though the victory at Warrington by a try to nil, was a very fortunate one. There were about 8000 spectators present when the teams entered the field under the charg., of Mr. Seddon, as referee. The following was the com- position of the teams :—Warrington : full back, nessam ; three-quarters, Carey, Potts, Evans, and Cunningham ; half backs, James T. Bate, and Clark ; forwards, Fair Turner, hlley, Buck- ley, Taylor, Berry, Dakin, Nevins, Thorniley. I—Rochdale Hornets : full-back, Wood ; three-quarter, Wightman,Midgley, Bowker, and Buckley ; half backs, Marshall and Chapman; forwards, Ashworth, Butter- worth, Dex, Horsefield, Simpson, Melledew, Trevor and Piggot. The Warrington team were donned in a new uniform in place of the familiar primrose and dark blue, and were not at the first moment or two recognisable to their supporters. A hearty cheer however was raised when it was discovered that the players in white jerseys with striped waistbands were the Warrington players. The Rochdale Hornets won the toss, and took advantage of a strong breeze which blew along the field from the railway end. The ball was set in motion by furrier whose kick-off was well returned by Buckley, to near half way. From the ensuing scrimmage the Warring- ton forwards made a grand dribble, and Woods only just saved in time. Warrington still pressed and a pass from Clark to Carey almost let the la ter in and a minute later Clark was held while in the act of grounding. The prolonged attack was at length brought to an end by the visitors conceding a minor. From the kick out, Chap- man secured and passed well to Marshall who ran to the half way flag where his career was cut short by Cunningham. Offside play by Chapman gave a free kick to Warrington. Turner's kick was well followed up by the forwards, and Woods had great difficulty in keeping them out. A good opening now presented itself to " Smack" Bate, but he was called back for some in- formality. Warrington rushed the scrimmage well and it would have gone hard with the"lnsects " had not Baw- ker stepped into the breach. A free kick to Chapman for an offside tackle gave his nide great relief and Heesnin was I called upon for the first time. Another free kick was awarded Rochdale,and Midgley's kick was returned well by Nevins to the quarter flas where Clark further gave his side an advantage by a free kick to half way. A flagrant peace of obstruction by the Hornets was riena- lized, but Turner's kick went backwards and Rochdale I almost got over, Cunningham being compelled to touch down. After the kick out, a brilliant bout of passing between Bowker and Buckley, ended in the latter being collared, but offside play by Jolley caused a free kick to be awarded against Warriag,ton in a most dangerous position. Bowker took the kick, and the ball just went outside the goal posts, and a second minor was scored. Wrightma.n Boon afterwards gained I a free kick which like Turner's also went backwards but nothing came of it. Taylor and Berry took the ball up the field when their efforts were neutralized by a free kick to Chapman who found touch at half way. This was very poorly returned by Cunningham, but Bate came to the rescue and by a grand run through his opponents, gained lost ground. A series of scrimmages now ensned near the iTornet's line, and at length, Bate taking smartly from Clark. scored under the posts. Potts kick at goal was a complete fiasco. After this reverse the Hornets played up and for a time they pressed, but the enthusiasm of Warrington spectators was roused to a high pitch by a passing movement which was the mast brilliant play of the day. Com- mencing with Nevins the ball passed in succession to Cunningham, Bate, Thornily, and Potts, the latter of whoM was tackled. A slight relaxation of Warrington was quickly taken advantage of by Rochdale and Wight- man taking a pass at top speed scored at the corner. Midgley landed a grand goal. From this time most exciting play followed up ta half time, and the Warrisg- ton team were buzzing like Hornets round the Hornet's goal. Nothing tangible turther took place however before half time, when the sccre was :—Hornets, one goal ; Warrineon, one try. After the interval Warrington went on with the determination to wipe out arrears and Taylor by a strong run almost got in, Woods tackling at the right moment. Buckley, Midgley, and Wightman by a passing movement gained a little ground which was lost again through the instrumentality of Bate and Clark. Ca(ey now accepted Bate's pass and galloping to the line he had the misfortune to be pushed into touch just on the line. Warrington were now pressing, and playing for all they were worth, but it appeared Impossible for them to get over. Time after time Bate, Clark. Potts and Cunningham were held on the line and the players were just getting disheartened when Cun- ningham accepting a pass from Bate just got over at the corner by a splendid run. The Hornets disputed the try on the ground that Cunningham had been in touch. The touch judge decided that he had not and the try was allowed. Turner's kick at goal did not come off Play now waxed furious, free kicks were frequent which somewhat sp iiled the game. Now of the free kicks however came off although the majority were not in unfavourable positions. The last ten minutes were of the most exciting description and Warrington appeared to be on the point of scoring several times. A loud shout arose when Nevins taking a sharp pass galloped over. It was with feelings of indignation that the referee's decision disallowing the try was received.. Fill time arrived shortly afterwards with the score : Warrington, two tries; Rochdale Hornets, one goal.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. STOCKPORT.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. STOCKPORT.

The football match with Warrington has now estab- lished itself as one of the main features of the " Wakes" at Stockport, and the match on Monday was in noways behind its predecessors in that respect. Unfortunately it rarely happens . that Warrington can raise their full strength against Stockport,and with the rising importance of the Stockport fifteen, it was all the more unfortunate that on this (eccasion the Warrington forward rank was not fully represented, such players as Timer, Dakin, Nevins, and Buckley being absentees. Four thousand spectators had assembled on Eigeley ground when J.lley set the field in motion. Favoured with a slight breeze but with the sun in their faces, Warrington pressed from the outset, as Pickaxe's return got no further than the guar- ter flag. Smith staved off any impending danger, but a penalty kick, entrusted to Evans, caused the play to remain where it was and from one of the scrim- mages Jolley was almost over. Bailey and Saville were the•firat to seriously test Warrington defence. Evans met their advance with a powerful punt which brought Smith into play. That player was at fault and a scrim- mage in front, of the home goal was the result. It was nicely worked in Warrington's favour, but Cunningham was too hasty in taking the pass and knocked forward. Hal it been accepted, the road was open. A further dis- appointment quickly followed, for Jolley was fiaored on the line at the earner fie,. What satisfaction there was . in seeing the visitors thus maintaining a strong but point- less attack was also short lived, far W. Bailey for the second time transferred the play. Heesom this time had difficulty in gathering the ball but Evans came to the , rescue. After a flying visit had been paid to Smith, the homesters again found footing in Warrington territory. ! Here a mistake on the part of Carey almost cost his side , dear. The play was going very fast when Carey getting clear-from the scrimmage made a sharpe but wild pass for it, fell into the wrong hands, and it was only the alertness of Heesom that prevented Saville getting in. Cunningham rendered effectual service by his strong fearlel tackling el the heavy Stockport forwards. The weak forward line of Warrington was further weakened , by Clark getting hurt and retiring, thus causing Berry to be called on to partner "Smack" Bate. The usually safe Stockport three-quarter,Bailey, was sadly at fault in the finishing touches a's he mulled an easy pass from Saville. ' It was well for Warrington that he did so as there was nothing between him and the scoring line. M tesev was almost equally at fault a few minutes later and as half- I time approached Evans made his mark in a good position but nothing came of it,and the teams crossed over with a clean sheet. Clark, though still suffering and unfit, resumed with the second half. The homestars early assumed the upper hand, Massey being the fiat to cause flees .en trouble. The tackling of the Warrineten enstedian coming as it did before Massey. ha I ant full steam lie, saved the nesilon hut his defence eentintiel to be sorely taxed. The first point was got throogta anything but brilliant play. Heesom made his mark close in from a Warrington man and during some little misippreheneion which fnllowed, Massey Yves al owed te steal away arid score. It seemed a d,,,ilyrui point, hut it wa.. allowed and Seville mede a spleedirl goel frean the try. A seened point was the enteemo of better play het i tee might have been prevented. After a short period Webster getting possession left al- opposition and romped in, Glover failing. div.head: NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON. HOW SOME PEOPLE LIVE.-SHOCKING DISCLOSURES.
div.p: NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON. HOW SOME PEOPLE LIVE.-SHOCKING DISCLOSURES.

On Friday week at the Warrington Borough Court before Alderman Wright (chairman), Messrs. J. W. Hayward and S. Wright, three cases of neg- lect of children were brought before the magis- trates at the instance of Inspector McAteer, N.S.F. C.C. In each case the worrier was sent to gaol for One month. Mr. J. D. Buckton prosecuted on be- half of the society. The first case heard was that of Richard and Elizabeth Tranter, 2, Warburton-street, who were charged with neglecting their five children in a manner likely to cause injury to health. Mr. Buckton said that was the third or fourth case from Warburton-street. It seemed to be the fashion there to let children grow up as best they could. In that case,the c,.othirg and bedding were filthy and the house was alss fiithy. 'Die male defen- dant had seven bird cages and auout ten birds. He had also two dogs. These were looked after even better than the children. He earned 355. a week. He gave his wife about 25.5. or 305. per week, and she seemed more to blame than her husband, owing to her drunken habits. But as long at the husband was at home he was responsible as Well as his wife. He was supposed to be the master of his house, and he should see that the children were not neglscSed. There 'vas always water and they could easily get soap and towel. Some of them seemed to think that once in four days was sufficiently often to wash their children.—lnspector McAteer stated that on the 14th of the present month in company with P.C. Dean he visited tne defendantis house He found the female prisoner in the kitchen and also the children. He examined the children and found them in a most deplorable state. The eldest girl, ten years of age, named Mary, was dressed with three old frocks. Her hair was matted together, and full ot knits and ver- min. George, aged seven, was iairly-well clothed, his flesh was dirty and his head and hair were in the same csndition as the girl Mary. Another boy rained James was in a similar condition. The child E izabeth was .lying on an old squab, dressed in a few filthy rags. It was also in a very dirty condition. Mrs_ Tranter was ' half-dressed and appeared as if she had not been washed for about three weeks. The kitchen was in a most dirty state. There was very li.tle furniture and no food of any description in the house. He went upstairs and where the defendants slept there was a bedstead with two old mattresses and a torn sheet. In the back room there were two mattresses on the floor saturated with urine and an old horse cloth for covering. The woman said her husband gave her 25s per we k. He afterwards saw the male defendant who told him that he earned 355. a week, and gave his wile 30s. out of it to maintain them. He said he didn't kitow what he could do with his wife. He was pu7, to such straits with the troubles caused by his wife that he had thought of taking the knife from the table and cutting his throat with it. Witness had visited the house five times and washed them several times before he took action. Each time he visited the house, instead of finuing it improving, he found it going worse. She was a drunken good-for- nothing woman. She was associated with other women in Warburton-st. who were drinking throughout the week In cross-examination witness said there were seven or eight birdcages in the house and ten birds. There was only one dog at the time of his last visit. P.C. Dean gave corroborative evidence as to the state of the house. —The male defendant said he worked every week, and did not call at a public-house once in six months. When he found his wife drunk he thrashed her for it. He had been working 17 years at his present situation, and had never been summoned here before in his life. Mrs. Tranter said the children had not been neglected. The magistrates committed her to gaol for one month and discharged her husband. George and Catherine Jaun Uri!, 6, Warburton-street, were charged with neglecting their four children. Mr. ,Buckton stated that the defendants had neglected their children in very snuch the same way as the other defend- ants. The bedroom was perhaps even in a worse condi- tion. They had a bed simply rotten with urine. The children slept on some rags and the rags were not only rotten it but the flair underneath was also rotten.— Inspector McAteer said that he visited the house on the ' 11th inst. in company with Inspector Cox and Constable Dean. The woman and her children were in the back kitchen. William, aged eight, was almost naked. He ' examined the child's body and found the fish i filthy. He did not think he had been washed for two or three weeks. The hair was matted and coveted with vermin. Florence, aged six, was dressed in two old frocks and was dirty. Hertoes were cut owing to the w-,ra-out shoes she was wearing. George, four years of age, was also in a dirty condition. His body was "picked" with the bites of vermin. The youngest child. Elizabeth, was only wear- ing one garment and had not been washed for a long time. In the defendant's bedroom there was simply nothing but an old bed or squab with two mattresses saturated right through with urine. The rooms were very dirty, and the smell was abominable. In the room where the children slept there were two sacks rotten with urine. Inspector Cox took his stick and removed theta a little and the boards underneath were also found to be rotten with dirt filth. It was outs of theworst cases he had ever seen since he joined the society. The house was not fit for a dog to lie in. He asked the woman how she accounted for it. She laughed at him,and said she couldn't tell. On the night of the 11th inst., the landlord turned them out through their dirty habits. The defendants took their children into a field where they slept for one night. The wife admitted to him that she had never sent the children to school. P.C. Dean gave evidence as to the state of the house. The defend- ant stated that he had not had enough work recently to keep the children in food. He had had to pawn the children's things and furniture in order to get food. The Chairman said the chief charge against him was that he had kept them in a filthy condition. The male defend- ant was then charged, and pleaded guilty to, keeping a dog without a license. P.C. Dean proved the case, and said he found the dog at the time of his visit to the defendant's house. The magistrates sentenced him to 14 days imprisonment for negle3t, and fined him ss. and costs for keeping the dog without a license, or in default a further period of imprisonment for seven days. His wife was committed to vac)l for one month:

John and Margaret Tulley, 9, Cropper's Brow, were charged with neglecting their child, Ellen. Mr. Buckton stated I.hat the husband was not so much to blame in that case as the wife. The man was both short-sighted and deaf and he believed that his wife took advantage of his infirmities. She had been at that court twenty times for drunkenness, prostitution, and theft. Inspector McAteer stated that on the 15th inst. in company with Detective Monaghan he went to the defendant's house. The woman and child were in the kitchen. There was no fire and practically nothing in the kitchen. The child was dressed in a few old rags. The housedid not appear to have been swept for twelve months. He could have gathered two or three stone of dirt from the floors,and it was in such a state as to be unfit for any man or woman to enter. The Chairman : It is a wonder the Sanitary Authority's officers have not visited them. The Inspector said lie thought there would be no harm if they did visit someof these houses .Onthe occasion of his second visit which was at night time he found no lieht in the house. The woman was lying on her back helplessly drunk with the child almost underneath her crying. The . husband soon afterwards came in and said he was afraid of her. She was a woman that was always drunk.Witneas had visited the house eight or nine times. It was no use speaking to her, she would simply do nothing. Witness was going down Buttermarkat-street a few days ago when he saw her sitting at the end of the street with some other women. She shouted to witness that she wanted him. He went towards her and she told hiin "I am not going fora pint. this time, but a quart." She had a quart jog in her hand and was going to fetch some beer. D. S. Monaghan said he was in company with the last witness on two occasions and what he had ated was correct. The male defendant worked for Mr. Greenough, soda water manufacturer.—Tully who had some difficulty in hearing what was said stated that his wages were nine shillings a week, but in the summer he got two shillings extra. Inspector McAteer stated that in justice to the male defendant he should state that Tully had visited witness'a office in refer- ence to his wife's conduct. He toll him that she had pledged the mattresses, and spent the money in beer.— ['he magistrates stated that they were very sorry for the husband and dismissed the case against him. His wife would be sent to gaol for one month. A case of neglec'. of children against John and Annie Barnes, 6. Cropper's Brew, was adjournud for a month in order that the wife might appear.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

A Church parson on the warpath against publi- cans! Such an announcement is enough to take away the breath of the "dumb dogs" of the Establishment in Warrington. And it is a curious coincidence that the name of this parson is Roberts. Ministers of the gospel of that name seem to be able to rise to the occasion when there is a bit of prac- tical Christianity to be carried out. On the whole, however, it will be admitted that it is much pleas- antez to accept the benefactions of liquor distillers than to put too fine a point on your Christian mision, especially as the sole condition is that you "wink the other eve" the song has it) at wholesale drunkenness and utter a few eulogistic platitudes when a wealthy brewer leaves this mortal sphere.

The "Woman's Signal" thus indignantly com- ments on the treatment which was received by the Churchman, Roberts :—" Can it be true in England that the citizen who dares to investigate criminal practices is made the criminal himself in court? It would seem so in the case of the Rev. Mr. Roberts, vicar of st. Clements, Notting Hill, who brought complaint against a publican for selling to a wan already drunk, and allowing him on hts premises. He was cross-examined as if he were the delin- quent instead of an independent and upright wit- ness. and failing to terrify him by such means, hi evidence being absolutely unshakable, a cheai laugh was raised at his expense by such questions as the following—Mr. Besley : How often have you been there ? I don't mean as a customer, but as a spy ?—Witness : Unc,.—MT.Besley : Ile has not yet subscribed to your charities? (Laughter.) The testimony given by the clergyman was supported by the police constable whom be had taken with him into the public-house ; but the court held that the publican was innocent as the man's condition was not brought to his notice, the drink having been sold by a servant or barman. If a publican's responsibility is settled by the wink of his eye, it will not encourage good citizens to demand or as- sist in the enforcement of law. And if their testi- mony and eye witness is to make them quasi of- fenders in reputable courts,there will be little hope of their bringing real offenders to justice."

The Continuation Schools were opened last week under very favourable circumstances. Their popu- larity appears to be growing year by year, and the present term promises to be far more successful than last. On Monday no fewer than 150 youthful students commenced their stulies, against 80 last year. In fact there were only 47 less than the total number who joinA during the whole of last season There were 50 students who were eligible for prizes, and Mr T. Morris in presenting them de- livered an encouraging address to them.

The St. John Ambulance Brigade which has been formed in Warrington is deserving of the ful- lest support. It is composed of members of the various S. John Ambulance classes in the town, and meetings are to be held for practice each week. A meeting -was held on Wednesday week when an emergency committee for carrying out the objects of the brigade was formed. Offers of assistance have already been made. Mr. Fair Turner offered to teach those mem- bers of the brigade who could swini,the art of saving the life of a drowning person, and Dr. Darwen, examiner of the St. John Ambulance Association, liondr,n, has promised to give a lecture. Of course the brigade is in need of funds, and it is thought that local employers of labour might lend a helping hand, seeing that the work of the brigade in rendering prompt action to injukol persons would be of value to teem, when liable for damages under the Employers Liability Act.

That was an awkward mistake which the local police marle the other day. A file-cutter was knocked up at three o'clock in the morning by two Policemen and escorted through the streets to the police station. This was what the Chief Constable called catching the bird before it awoke. But as a matter of fact this bird should not have been caught at all. The man was apprehended under the , belief that a fine which had been imposed for not sending his children regularly to school had not been paid, although as it was found out afte,rwards it had been paid all the tim?. Police accounts should be carefully kept, seeing that mistakes lead to such disagreeable results.

The municipal elections are still armsing very slight interest in Warrington. Not a single move has been made by either political party, and the Trades Council, after choosing one candidate now rests from its labours for a time. Should there be contests all round, it will come rather heavy upon two of the retiring Conservative members of the Council who have gone in at bye-elections. .Coun- cillor Baird had an arduous stiuggle in the Bewsey ward in November last, and although beaten there, he entered the Council shortly afterwards after a severe struggle in the Otford ward. Councillor Evans has also only attended a single Council meet- ing, and had to fight for that.
FARLIN.

The almost continu ii cry of " Ser-imps, set-imps, floe set-imps. a penny a jilt, a penny a ,jill," on the blessed 6ahbatti day, is very annoying. Could not something he done to abate this nuisance woich we have to endur° throughout what ought to be a quiet day of rest? Runcorn.

RtrOBY FOOTBALL.

Warrington have gained their first two points in the Lancashire Rugby League, but it was only by the bare majority of one point. As a result of this% they are among the first four. The match on Saturday was an even closer game than the one b,tween the same com- batants last year. when our local team won by a try to ail. The scorer of that try,Taylor, was,in the team this year, but he did not repeAt his performance of charging down the full back's kiek, and racing half the length of the field, although he played exceedingly well.

Before coming.to the players of Saturday's match, I will give the results of the matches between the other teams which composed the League en Saturday. Oldham were in a scoring mood, and they obtained three goals, two tries at the expense of Broughton Rangers,the latter scoring a goal and a try in rettarn. Swinton are falling into evil times, for on Saturday they suffered their second successive defeat. Tyldesiey were the team to extract two points out of the" Lions,' which they did by the same majority of points aci Warrington obtained over Rochdale Hornets. Wigau are commencing the season as they did last. They scored a goal and three tries to Salfecd nil, and appear to be a very dangerous team indeed. St. Helens and Leigh have each to rna4te their blw in the League competition. the latter of whom will have a rest until they meet Warrington on December 2nd. The following is the result of the competition up to data : .

_ For. Ara. PM. Won. Lost. Dm. G. T. G. T. Pts. Oldham Tyldesley Warrington Wigsn. St. Helens 0 C 0 0 0 0 ... '0 0 ... 0 Broughton Rangers 1 ... 0 ... 1 ... 0 ... 1 1 .- 3 2 ... 0 Salford Swinton Rochdale Hornets *frigh * Leigh have been suspended till the •end of November for prdessionalism.

At the match on Saturday it cannot be denied that the victory of six points to five did not represent the difference between the two teams. Warrington were far and away the better team, and were pressing three , parts of the game. They were, however, sadly wanting in finishing touches to their movements. They ought to have scored at least three or foul- tries more than they did, but somehow or other, after most 'brilliant play in the open, they failed when near the line. Nevins had the hardest'lines of all, for he actually gat over at the end of the game, and was greaUy surprised when he was called baeeby the referee. also think that a little practice in goal kicking would not be a very bad thing. With the exception of these two faults, the.Warrington team played a grand game on Saturday, and were the complete masters of their opponents.

Coming to the players, I consider that Heesom fully maintained his reputation for accurate 'tackling, and fielding. On the opposite side, Woods also proved a good custodian. The Hornets;three-quarter line were slightly in advance of Warrington. They had two very brilliant men in Bowker and Buckley. For Warrington, Evans though not brilliant was as safe as ever. Cun- ningham when he gets a tittlemore experience w!ll ne a decided acquisition to the Warrington ranks. He has a high turn of speed which proved very useful on Satur- day in getting the second try. Potts was very erratic and his kick at goal from a try scored under the posts was a complete failure. 'Carey did not do anything sensational on Saturday, although he had hard lines once or twice in being pushed into touch just as he got to the line. The rival half 'bailts were very evenly matched. " Smack " Bate however.was the best The ex-Barrow men are a decided acquisition to Rochdale, and but for them, the Hornets would have had a much warmer time of it than they had. The Rochdale for- wards have retrograded since last year. At that tinge they were almost the best in Lancashire, but they are but an ordinary lot this year. Conspicuous among the Warrington forwards were Turners Jolley, Taylor and Berry.

Warrington had to suffer defeat on Monday at the hands of Stockport, by a goal and a try to nil. At the corresponding match last year, Stockport obtained two goals to Warrington a try. Warrington had the misfor- tune to lose Clark who was injured. The Stockport team have improved wonderfully during the last year or twa, and take some beatinz on their own ground. They are serious rivals to Runcorn in their claim to the dignity of champions of Cheshire, and on Saturday they drew with them.

To-day, the Warrington team have their work cut out for them. They have to meet the Oldham team at the capital of Spindiedom. As that team have been carrying all before them thus far, it will be a feather in the cap of Warrington if they can check their mad career. Warrington are relying upon the following team to uphold their honour: Full back. Heesolt. ; three•quarter hacks, Cunningham, 'Potts, Evans and Carey: half backs, James T. Bate and Clark ; forwards. Fair Turner, Jolley, Taylor, Berry, Thorniley, Dakin, Nevins, Buck- ley. It is to be hoped that this team will be competent to hold the Oldham team at bay if it does nothing else.

The " A "team were not so successful in their efforts on Saturday as fweeretheir seniors on the Wilderspool ground. They journeyed to hilly Mossley to play the Mossley Brow team, a team,which by the way,is coming to the front,since the Mossley team became defunct. A little mistake made by two of the Warfington players , at Manchester Station, as to the time of the departure of the train for Mossley, caused the Warrington team to be two men short at the kick-off, and for the earlier part of the game the Mossley men had the best of matters in consequence, but were unlucky in not scoring. The platy throughout cannot he described as brilliant, as it was of a scrambling nature. Scrimmages were far too frequent, and many opportunities for scoring were missed by both teams. The sound of the whistle f.,r no- side came as a relief. Neither side scored a major point, and the match therefore resulted in a draw. To-day the A" team are to play their first engagement in the club championship matches for "A" teams when their oppon- ents will be the Oldham 4-‘ A" team.

I notice that the Excelsiors proved the masters of Tranniere "A " 135 four tries to nil. By the way, they appear to be badly in want of a goal kicker. Not a single goal out of four attemota, does not say much for the cuiality of those the have got. If they could not kick goals themselves, however, they did not allow the other side to have a try whether they could do :46.4r not. The Excelsiors hive thus far proved invincible and I hope that th 27 will prove a good nursery ground for the senior teams.

Another team which is in want of a goal kicker is the Stockton Heath team. They actually scored six tries against Ainscough and never a goal could they obtain. As the Heathens are going so well this season, and St. Mary's the cup holders are doing likewise, it will he a rare fight between the two next Saturday,and I should not like to pick the winner.

I have seen a fixture card of the Warrington Rangers who commenced serious operations on •Saturday at Run- corn, where they met the Recreation team of that town. They are again running two teams, and have an excel- lent list of fixtures. J. Monks and A. Scholze are the respective captains of the -first and second teams. They meet. both St. Mary's and Stockton Flea.* and the" A" teams of a good number of the surrounding leading clubs. They will have to forego the pleasure of going to Leigh on November 3, however from very well-known reasons.

WATER POLO. The Warrington team are carrying everything before them, and on Monday night by the decisive majority of five goals to one over S.)uthport, they entered the final stage of the competition for the Liverpool and District Cup. They have surmountql all obstacles thus far, but the last fence is a high one, for they have to meet St. Helens in the final. lam not without hope that they will accomplish the task of beating even this team, and thus in their first season be able to proclaim themselves the champions of the Liverpool District. Telly have played so consistently of late that this is well within the range of possibility.

The match on Monday was an excellent one, but after the game had got into full swing, there was only one team in it and that was not Southport. Locker had quite a mania for scoring goals, and four out of the five were from his hands, the other being scored by Jones. Fair. Turner had extremely hard lines, for he hit the goal post time after time. The whole of the Warrington players, in fact, were the con.plete masters of their op- ponents. Southport had a very good goalkeeper, or it would have gone hard with them.

Mr. William Belly, a well-kno-an Freemason, has left £5,000 for old-age pensions under Corporation manage- mint at Leicester. The Belfast papers publish the details of a sensational elopement of an Arraagh clergyman's daughter, who is alleged to have disappeared a few days ago with a farm servant employed in the neighbourhood of her father's rectory. It was reported to the City of London Commission 4.f Sewers that during the past two months thirty-six t-ns of meat had been seized and condemned in the markets of the Corporation.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 29, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 29, 1894.

div.head: WARRINGTON ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS:
div.p: WARRINGTON ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS:
ANOTHER LICENSE REFUSED.

The adjourned licensing sessions for the borough of Warrington were held at the Police Court on Thur,day morning. There was again a large attendance of the public, among those present being the Revs, E. T. Reed, W. H. Drummond, and D. W. Roberts, G. D. Mason, and W. J. Kirkland, and Messrs, W. Roberts, W. J. Shaw, W. Diggle, and R. Storey. The following were the magistrates present :—Mr. John Fairclough, lir. F. Monks, Alderman Francomb, Alderman Wright, Mr. W. Pierpoint, Councillor Roberts, Mr .1. H. Fleming, Mr, J. W. Hayward, Mr. T. Birchall, Mr. E. J. Guest, Alderman Sutton, Mr. J. Burgess, Mr. S. Wright, Mr. E. Garnett, Mr. L. Voisey. Messrs •Greenall, Whitley and Co., were represented by Mr. T. Swift, barrister, and Mr. R. Davies, and Mr. Arthur Browne also appeared on behalf of several licenses. Mr. Tobin, barrister, Liverpool, appeared on behalf of Messrs. Bishop and Co., and other objectors to certain applications.
NEW APPLICATIONS. THE BOROUGH ARMS.

Mr. R. Davies said tbast he was instructed to make an application to their worships, and he did not wish to touch upon any subject of controversy. Mrs. Elizabeth Riley, widow of John Riley, occupied a house in sight of that court, at the corner of Mersey-street. She had kept it since her husband's death with great credit to herself, and he did not think it was necessary to appeal to her character before the magistrates, all of whom possibly knew something about her. She thought that the house was rather small,and the only accommodation for witnesses at the sessions held at that court was to go to the house at the corner. Mrs. Riley was therefore desirous of having an enlargement of her premises, and to have a fully licensed house with the consent of the owner, Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. Be wished to impres up in their worships that there was not proper aecemmodation for the people who waited outside the court in the ram, nor for wittlesses, solicitors, or others who had no room to go to. If there was a room in the court, it would be another matter, but the magistrates had no roam for themselves. Some of the magistrates might smile, but it was not for a pecuniary advantage that the present application was made. The sole object of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. was to improve their houses. They were willing to lay out money to make their houses more comfortable. As to the wants of the neighbourhood, there was an extensive popula- tion, in Irlam-st., Mersey-st., and Howley-lane, and a respectable house for those people was in his opinion desirable. If the magistrates would grant the full license to the house, Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. were willing to give up the Harp and Crown in return. If that were done, within three years' time, five licensesi woold be given up by the Company, which would cause a diminution of existing licenses, which some people ' were so anxious should take place. Elizabeth Riley, the applicant, said that she had her- self kept the house for eleven years, and had had no , complaint during the whole of that period. She wished to have a better house and that was the cause of her ' present application.--Cross-examined by Mr. Tobin: She had never managed a fully licensed house. She did not know how many fully licensed houses there were already within 200 yards. She supposed that the Harp and Crown did much less business than her own house; in f-itt, there was no comparison.—Re-examined : She was frequently asked for spirits. Mr. Wm. Owen, architect, then produced plans of the building, and also of the proposed alterations. He said that he did not consider that there was suffieient aclom- modation at present. With the present house improved, I.he thought it would be a very good thing for the neigh- bourhood. With the improvements contemplated, wit- ness considered that roughly a sum of £4OO or £5OO would be required, besides the loss of two cottages.— Mr. Tobin: Do you say it is to the pecuniary advantage .of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. to have the extra accommodation? No.—Then this application will re- sult to the pecuniary disadvantage of Messrs. Greenall, -Whitley and Co.? I think so. Mr. It. Davies interrupting said he had stated the company's object was to improve their property, and not for any pecuniary advantage in the way of sale of intoxicating liquor. Evidence of the respectability of the house was given by Thomas Moores,Alf red Downes, and Charles Jackson. Mr. Davies was proceeding to call other witnesses to give similar evidence, when Mr. ToL,in interrupting,said that he thought it was quite unnecessary, as he made no charge a.ainst the conduct of the house. Mr. R. Wynne Jones. a director of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and 00., said that they did not expect any pecu- niary advantage from the alteration as the company had no interest in the sale of spirits.—Mr. Davies : You are aware that the magistrates have gone round all the houses in the town, either themselves or by deputy, and have made certain requirements which have caused you to lav not money? Yes.—But you are ready to carry out their suggestions? Yes. Mr. Tobin s.id that it was stated by Mesars.Greenall, Whitley and Co., that they wished to give more conveni- once to Witileg4PS and magistrates who attended the court. They said that they wished it in the interest of the magistrates, who sat on the bench daily. (Laughter.) Why could they not get a magistrate to come forward and go into the box to say so ? They had not a single witness to that effect. __

Mr. Davies: There was Mr. Owen. Mr. Tobin said that Mr. Owen did not speak as a mar,istrate, but as an architect, and he did not state whether he had ever been inconvenienoed. If Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. were so anxious to conveni- ence the magistrates, why did they not provide a room now ? and he did not think that the magistrates would wish so much for a fully licensed house, but would be content with a newspaper. Mr. Davies: I never mentioned magistrates using the house. Mr. Tobin (reading): I have got down witnesses, legal gentlemen, and I certainly took down magistra' es. This is an outrageous argument. Continuing, Mr. Tobin said that in granting a new license, the magistrates were not hound by any consideration, applying to an old license. ThPy all knew the wants of the neighbourhood, and it was his opinion that a reduction of licenses was wanted. With regard to the offer to close the Harp and Crown, they would have one fully licensed house instead of two heerhouses. The result would he an increase of business. The Company would give up absolutely nothing. The old Harp wis dying. Let it die out. He proposed to call Mr. Fleming, the manager of Messrs. Bishop and Co.'s borax works, who objected to the application as a ma.nufarturer. Mr. Fleming was then called and said that the borax works were not far from the Borough Arms. He employed 30 men at the wrrks, besides contractors. fie aid not consider that a fully licensed house was r$ quired as there were 3 g6ind many others about the district.—By Mr. Davies: He had been in Warrington three years. His teen would .not necessarily go to the Old Crow if they required drink. He had come to the court to speak for himself. He thought that the facilities for drinking spirits were clearly sufficient in the neigh- hourligod. He objected also because men were made drunk sooner by spirits than by beer. Mr. Davies said that he might inform the manistrates that Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., were willing to alter their plans as the magistrates thought most desir- able.

div.head: GREEN MAN.
div.p: THE GREEN MAN.

Benjamin KenvonT of the Green Man beerhouse, Green-street, applied for a wine license for selling on and off the premises. He said that he had served the notices as requ'red by law.—No one appeared to object to the application. APPLICATIONS FOR MUSIC LICENSES. Mr. Arthur Browne applied on behalf of Henry Row- ley, of the Unicorn Inn, for a music license. He said that his client merely wished to protect himself, and only intended to occasionally have singing in his house. James Burrows, Queen's Hotel, Sankey-st., also ap- plied for a music license. He said that the:concert hall was in the old Masonic rooms. Mr. Arthur Browne applied fora music license for the Whit. Bull. He said that his client, Mrs. Balshaw, was treated unfairly at the last music licensing sessions, as they had no notice whatever that the license would be refu,ed. There was sufficient supervision over the house. The magistrates then retired, and after about half an hour's absence, they returned, and Mr. Fairclough said that it had been decided to refuse all the applications. ADJOURNED LICENSES. THE PELICAN INN.

Mr. Swift said he appeared to ask the magistrates to grant the renewal of the license of the Pelican Inn to the new tenant. Their Worships would remember that on August 23, the date of the annual licensing meeting, they gave the subject a very full inquiry. He need not go into that again, but the end of that inquiry was that they adjourned the case until that day. Since then,the old licensee Allen, had removed from the house entirely, and given up the premises. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley. and Co. had obtained a new tenant, Fairfield Thompson Turner, who was now the tenant and occupier of the premiscs, and was now carrying on the business in virtue of a temporary authorit•y granted by some of the mar..,istrates of the court. Mr. Turner was extremplv well known in Warrington, and also very much res- pected. The Head Constable also gave him an excellent character. Mr. Turner was a married man, and he was prepared to attend to the business and conduct it in a proper manner. He was not going to apply for a singite, and dancing lieense,nor would he allow it upon his pre- mises. He trusted the magistrates would have no diffi- culty about renewing the license. The Chief Constable on being called, said that Mr. Turner bore a good character, and the police had no objection to the renewal of the license. Fair. Turner was then called ,and gave formal eridence of taking the house.—Cross-txamined by Mr. Tobin : He had never kept a public-house before. He did not live at the Pelican at present. The rent was £34. Mr. Tobin said that as the magistrates had tdinurned the case, his instructors could only guess at the reason why the case was adjourned, and that was, that the

man Allen, who was not called at the last inquiry,owing he believed to illness, would be called at the adjourned date. In the meantime temporary authority had been granted to Turner, who now applied for the renewal. He contended that if Allen WaS good enough to apply for the licenselast time, he was good enough now. But the objection was to the house—that it was not carried on in a proper manner, and that improper things had been committed in the house. He objected to this whitewashing, so to speak, of a house, by putting in a man against whom nothing could be said. 'The evidence against the house was no doubt frEsh in their Worship's minds, and he hoped th‘y would refuse the license. Mr. Swift contended tha:: nothing improper had been done in this case by a new tenant applying tor the license, as sufficient notice had also been given by the notices served upon the Head Constable, and the magi... trates' clerk, and the magistrates themselves. There as no objection on account of any conviction. Mr. Swift was proceeding t) deal with the evidence of the last session, but Mr. Tobin objected, and the Clerk ruled Mr. Swift out of ord2r, whereupon that gentleman retorted. "If lam ruled out,l know how to sit down" (Laughter).

div.head: WOOLPACK.
div.p: THE WOOLPACK.

Mr. White said that with r.gard to the Woolpack there was no objection,coisequently they had no cour,e but. to renew it. They might however mike aorne suggeftion with reference tf.) the steps upon which the unfortunate occurrence took place a short time ago.

div.head: TRH DECISION.
div.p: TRH DECISION.

The magistrates retired tor about half an hour, and on their return, it was announced dint the license for the Pelican had been refused, and the magistrates recom- mended that the steps of the Woolpack in Bold-street be renr.ved.
Mr Arthur Browne promised to bring the suggestion as to the Wootpack before his clients. This concluded the business.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES- WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES- WARRINGTON.
WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

A well-attended meeting of this society was held on Sunday at ernoon. Mr. Kershaw, of Wa rrington, who occupied the chair, delivered a brief address on progress, passing in review several progressive mo vetnents of the Present day, in which he included the P S.A. movement. Mr. Ness, of Manchester, was the speaker for the after- noon and based his remarks on the text "We are brothers one of another," Romans 12 c., sv. Miss Cos- grove was the soloist and sang extteedingly well a hymn and "The Lost Chord." The Rev. J. Ytlnge, Messys. D. Owen. and G. Morrell also took part in the meeting. WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.

Special services were held at this church on Sunday, when colleetions were taken on behalf of the mainten- ance fund. The Rev. J. Yonge was the preacher, morn- ing and evening. The choir under the conductorship of Mr. G. Wallington rendered the anthem "I will extol Thee," (Fludion), at the morning service. In the even- ing the chair also sang two anthems vic.: " By Bah 5 lon's Wave," (G)Unod),and "0 Saviour of the W0r1d,"(6045). There were large congregations, and the amount required, £3O, was realised:

div.head: BOWLING
div.p: BOWLING
HANDICAP AT CROFT.

On Saturday -3.-f-t;:r-nWon-,- the iil-eCribers of the Horse Shoe Inn Bowling Club. Croft, met at the inn and plAyed their closing same for the season en the home green. the Committee and officers bad arranged a handicap for a number of prizes consisting of money and articles. About ZO members competed, the game being eleven up, and the green being in excellent condition sem° fine bowling took place. At the conclusion, the members ' and friends sat down to a knife and fork tea, served by the host and hostess. Mr. and Mrs. MAines. During the evening the president of the club, Mr. G. Brimelo% presented prizes to the successful competitorv. The following is a list of the prizA-winners t-1, W. Lrthgoe, Bs.; 2, C. Allen 64. 3, W. F. Pennington, 54.; 4, W. Straw, 4s. ; 5, d. Kent, 33. : 6, T. Houghton, 2a. ed. ; 7. IW. Maines, Is. 61. The consolation prizes for players thr4wn out of the first round were net finished, and the prizes were, therefore, not awarded. WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVE CLUB. ANNUAL MAIN.

The last. stages of the bowling main were brought to a close on Saturday afternoon, the final in the consolation prize between Mr. F. Horahin and Mr. W. W. Westwell having to be played in the dark. The prizes were dis- tributed in the first-class billiard room by Mrs. Francomb about 7.50. The list of peze-winners is as follows prize, Mr. W. Cooper; 2nd, Mr. W. Wilcoc ks ; 3rd, Mr. C. Oldfield ; 4th, Mr. Billinge ; sth, Mr. Woods ; Gth,Mr. T. Bridge; 7th, Mr. W. Hill; Bth, Mr. W. Millington. Consolation Priv-s: Ist, Mr. T. Horahin ; 2nd, Mr. W. W. Westwell; 3rd, Mr. T. Cooper ; 4th. Mr. T. Ogden ; sth, Mr. Webb ; 6h, Mr. J. Taylor; 7th, Mr. Gibson; tth, Mr. J. Thornton. The SECRETARY of the Bowling-green Committee (Mr. T. Mason) proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Francomb for her presence and for distributing the prizes. Mr. ruostrrobt seconded the motion.which was carried unanimously. Alderman FaaNcossa, in responding on behalf of Mrs. Prancomb, said it tiad given his wife great pleasure to come there that evening, as she tcsik a great interest in everything appertaining to the Conservative Club. He begged to thank them very heartily for the vi te rf thanks winch had been passed to his wile. (Appsause.) A vote of thanks was accorded to the manager and manageress of the club (Mr. and Mrs. Watkins). In replying to a vote of thanks to the Bowfin,/ Green Committee, proposed by Alderman Francomb, Mr. Join; ROBERTS (chairmen of that committee) said he had been chairman for several years, and he had never worked with a 'better committee. (Applause.) The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: ASTON.
div.p: ASTON.

PRESENTATION TO TSB REV. EDWARD MARSDEN.—.-OD Thursday eveni,pg a very interesting presentation took place in the National SP,hools, Aston, when the Rev. Edward Marsden, vicar of St. Peter's Church was made the recipient of a silver salver and a chequ. The occa- sion was the jubilee of his connection with the village, which exhibited quite an animated scene in the evening. At six o'clock there was a tea,g'ven by the Rev. Edward Marsden and his wife, to which 300 residents in the district had been invited. At the conclusion of the re- past the rev, gentleman was pvsented with :he sAlver and cheque,and several speeches were delivered by some of the most well-known parishioners. The Rev. Edward Marsden, who is a son of the late Vicar of Eccles, and is about 78 years of age, took over the living of St Peter's Aston,in September, 1844, at which time lie was a curate under the late Canon Greenall of Stretton. During his connection with the district of As on he lias been iiptru- mental in performing a great amount of good work and is generally loved and respected. For 30 years t-,e was chaplain of Dutton Workuouse, and for a long period filled the position of Chairman on the Aston United Dis- trict School Board of which he has been a member since its creation. Big public beneficial acts have been many, and wtken subscriptions were being solicited by Mrs. Flervey'Talbot and several of her friends, not a single refusal was met with ; everyone in the district gave their utmest with pleasure. The amount re-iliz,d was about £BO, which, in itself, is sulffeient to show t he popularity of the rev. gentleman. To-night (Friday) a tea will he given to all the Sunday school children of the neighbourhood by the Rev. Edward Marsden and his wife.

UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES. At the Training C illege on Wednesday evening there was a large addience, consisting clii,fly of lady students at the Training College and Clergy Diugh- ters School, to hear Mr. C. E. Mallet, 8.A., of Baliol College, Oxford, deliver tbe first of a series of six lectures on "The Tudors." The Rev. Morley Steven- son, in introducing the lecturer, stated that an arrangement had been made whereby they were enabled for the first time to present two courses of University lectures in the year instead of one as formerly. He hoped they would all see at once the gain of that, Ode course would be held at the Training College, and the other in another part of the t.)wn. It had been pointed out that the present course of lectures was likely to clash with a course they had eighteen months ago on the Reformation, but in the present cow's() there was only one lec- ture which dealt with the reformation in the Eng- lish church, so that they would have five lectures out of the six which broke entirely fresh ground. Mr. Mallet then proceeded with his lecture, which waq interesting and instructive. He dealt with the adinini-tration of Chrdinal Wolsey. A class was held after the lecture.

div.head: WA It RINGTON.
div.p: WA It RINGTON.

GOOD TEMPLARY AT LATCHFORD. • On Monday evening a special session ot the Bone- hill Branch Lodge of the Independent Order of Good Tempters was held in the 'Temperance Hall, under the presidency of Bro. B. Walker, Chief Templar. There was an excellent attendance,many visitors and friends being present. The programme was of a routine character, consisting ot songs, readings, recitals, &c. the following taking part : Bros. F. Blease, E. Cliffe, W. Owen, F. Pearson, B. Walker, and :Aster L. Hough. Before closing Bros. H. Richardson and B. Few gave encouraging addresses, the latter describing his travels in many lands. The meeting terminated by singing and prayer.

div.head: FIRE AT MESSRS. RYLANDS BROS.
div.p: FIRE AT MESSRS. RYLANDS BROS.

About 345 on Saturday morning a slight-flre was discovered in the second storey of Messrs. Rylands Bros.' Wire Works,Cturch-st. The fire brigade was immediately sent for, but on their arrival the fire nad been practically got under by the workmen. By some means the ceiling of the second storey be- gan to smoulder, and the ventilator had acted like a chimney anti drawn all the flames to it, the result being the destruction of the ventilator. Beyond this very little damage had been done. CONCERT IN AID OF Sr. ANN'S CHURCH CHOIR. On Monday evening an excellent concert in aid of St. Ann's choir took place in the schoolroom, Dannett-street, before a fair audience. A good pro- gramme was prepared, the artistes being Miss M. Taylor, Miss R. Rigbey, Miss Milne, Miss R. Ta)lor, Mest,rs. C. Higg-, J. Seed, F. Taylor, and W. Whittle. The band, conducted by Mr. Percy Randall, per- formed selections of music during the evening. A vote of thanks to the performers, proposed by the Rev. J. Davies, brought the conc-rt to a conclusion. "AT HOME" TO SCHOOL TEACHERS.

On Saturday afternoon, an "At Home" was given to the day school teachers of Warrington and dis- trict, by Mr. and Mrs. W.Long, J.P., at their house, Thel wall Heyes. A good number were taken there by a conveyance provided by Mr. Connor.. The afternoon was spent in a very pleasant manner, croquet, bowls, nioundards, and other games being much enjoyed. Refreshments were also provided, and during the afternoon Mr. Pearson's band was in attendance. Songs were contributed by Mr. Dewhurst and Mrs. Stansfeld. A most enjoyable afternoon was brought to a close at six o'clock,after a vote of thanks had been accorded to Mr. and Mrs. Lang for their kindness.

div.head: BANE QUAY WORICINGMBN'S MISSION BAND OP
div.p: BANE QUAY WORICINGMBN'S MISSION BAND OP
HOPB.

The Band of Hope Society in connection with the above mission, opened their present season on Saturday, when they partook of a first class tea in the schoolroom, provided by the young ladies of the society. There was a very fair attendance at t e tea, and the numbers were greatly increased at the entertainment which was provided afterwards. Miss Bessie Dutton, who preshied,gaye a very inspiriting address to the young members present. MIBB Fur- ness, and Miss Edith Lawton gave excellent recita- tions, and clarionet solos were ably given by Mr. A. Aderofr. Mrs. Joseph Monks sang "Killarney" in an excellent and pleasing manner. Mr. Milling- ton was also successful in his song" Laugh and grow fat." A pianoforte duet was very ably given by MifiB Eva and Master J. P. Pilling. The latter also gave a pianoforte solo, entitled "t he sailor's dream," in an excellent manner. Mr. F. Atkinson was accorded the heartiest applause for his render- ing of two comic songs accompanied by himself on the banjo. The rendition of the dialogue, "Wildair's Birthday," brought a most successful evening to a close.

div.head: WARRINGTON ODDFRLLOWI SUPPER.
div.p: WARRINGTON ODDFRLLOWI SUPPER.

The officers and members of tile committee of the Odgellows Juvenile Society sat down at the White Bull Inn, florsemarket-street, the other night, to a supper which had been provided for them by the hostess (Mrs. Balshaw). The toast "Success to the Juvenile Burial Society" having been drunk, the secretary (Bro. Pownall) said he had very much pleasure in b4.ing able to give such a good report of the society. Since it started in 1868 (26 years ago), 448 death claims' which amounted to X1,44016..61., had been paid. There was at the present time a membership of 850, and a capital account of £1,427 lie. 841., invested as follows :—With the Warrington Corporstiqn, £1,000; in the Warrington Savings Bank,.Elso ; Warrington Medical As-nciation, .£150; district. fund, £100; and £27 lie. Bd. in the trea- surer's hands. Each member was then presented with a fine portrait of the officers and members of the, committee, which had been executed by and refl-cted great credit on the artist, Mr. Birtles, of Sinkey-st. The rest of the evening was spent in a convivial manner, Bros. Pownall, Appleton, Alcock, Cross. and Joynson rendering songs, readings, &c., and the evening was brought to a close by the sing- ing of the National Anthem. CHESHIRE LINES ENGINEERS PICNIC.

The rnemb-nis of the Cheshire Lines engineers department had a picnic to Halton Castle on Satur- day. On their arrival a bowling main was played by the visitors, the prize-winners being as follows : —First prize, silver medal (to he won two years in succes,don), Charles Ashbrook ; 2. silver teapot, H. Jordan ; 3 bottle of champagne. F. B Page; 4, cruet stand, C. Birch; 5. spoons G. Longshaw ; 6, watch, T. Holdcroft ; 7. watch chain, G. Higham ; 8, night alarm, C. Newall ; 9, sleeve-links. W. Moine; 10, automatic hank. S. Turner; 11, solitair?s. W. Hi“ham ; 12. puzzle. D. Plinston ; 13, breast-pin, F. Sinclair; 14, pocket-knife, C. Sinclair; 15. rattle, J. Ward; 16. whip, A. Driver ; 17, hunter's knife. G. Harding; 18, hat guard. S. Hackett. A first-class knife and fork tea WAS done full justice to, and a very enjoyable evening was spent, so,ngs and recita- tions beinQ given by Messrs. D. Plinston, G. Higharn W. Highara, H. Jordan, F. and C. Sinclair, &c. Thanks were given to the host and to Messrs D. Plinston and G. Higharn for their services.

div.head: MEETING OF TEE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.
div.p: MEETING OF TEE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.

On Monday afternoon the monthly meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce was held in the rooms of the Secretary, Councillor A. Bennett, arket Gate Chart-hers. 4 letter was read from the Postma.ter-General in reply to the suggestion of the Warrington Chamber that envelopes of a dis- tinctive colour should he used for telegrams ad- dressed to the care of second persons. He stated that owing to various departmental difficulties the shE.Yge,tion could not be entertained. We under- stand that the proposal has received the support of other influential Chambers, and it, is the general opinion that its adoption would prevent mistakes and he a considerable convenience to the commer- cial community. Communications were read in favour of imperial contribution to the proposed inter-colonial line of fast mail steamers; but whilst the idea was regarded with favout, no formal action wa44 taken in the matter. The Secretary (Mr. A. Bennett) reported that. a suggestion recently made by the ChambFr to the eff-iet that the British Navy might he recruited from the industrial schools of the country had been officially brought forward by the Newcastle Chamber at .the recent autumnal meeting of the Associated Chambers at Hudders- field. The Secretary was instructed to write to the Mansion House Association on Railway and Canal Traffic, complaining in reference to certain difficul- ties experiencEd by local manufacturers as to the result of present arrangements in regard to terminal charges.

div.head: DETERMINED SUICIDE : DROWNED IN A RAINTUB.
div.p: A DETERMINED SUICIDE : DROWNED IN A RAIN- TUB.

An inquest was held at the Police Station on Tuesday, Ny Mr. F. A. .Tones, upon the body of Ann Charnock, widow, aged 75 years, who committed suicide the same morning by drowning herself in the rain-tub.—Wm. Charnock, 49, Napier-street, said that deceased was his mother and resPed with him. She had been almost bedfast for eleven months previous to her death, and she was under the care of Dr. Peacocke. She suffered from general debility. He had no reason to believe that she would take away her own life. Ile last saw her alive at iO3O on Monday night when she was in bed. At about 4.45 on Tuesday morning, witness , heard an unusual noise in the back-yard, and on 'going to see what it was, be found his mother in the rain-tub, which was full of water. A step lad- der had been placed against it. Witness pulled her out, and took her into the house. As she appeared to be dead, he went for the police who also brought Dr. Peacocke. The doctor at once pronnunced life to be extinct. Deceased must have placed the step- ladder against the rain-tub. It, must have been a great struggle for the deceased to get out at all, as she was very feeble. She appeared to have gone into the rain-tub head first.—Beattice Rowlands, granddaughter of the deceased, said that shs slept with her grandmother on Monday night, hut she never heard her get out of bed.—The jury returned a verdict that the deceased committed suicide while of unsound mind.

div.head: WARRINGTON MINTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON MINTY COURT.

CLAIM AGAINST A BUILDER.-At the Warrington County Court. on Thursday, Mr. E. A. White, selicitor, claimed on behalf of Lord Lilford from Jol n V. Lloyd, builder, Bank Quay, the immediate possession of a barn aria land in Mill-lane, Sankey, the term of which had ex- pired, also £1 ss. for quarter's rent due, and a further sum of £9 10i. for breach of defendant's contract to fence off the south side of the defendant's premises. Mr. White stated that the defendant had 1( r several years occupied these premises under the plaintiff. At the defendant's expressed request an agreement for a ten- ancy for three months was agreed to, the defendant un- dertaking to erect a fence within three months. That time had expired and the defendant had not done the fencing, and had also not given up possession, and was still holding possession. He asked his Honour for an order for possession forthwith, and for the rent due. The charge for feecing was based at ss. per yard, but that was for an iron fence. The plaintiff would be content with a wooden fence.—Mr. John Selby stated that he was an estate agent in the employ of his father who was agent for Lord Lilford. The agreement produced was signed by the defendant, who was made liable to fence off the south side of the land in question. It was still unfenced off, and the defendant held possession.—Mrs. Lloyd appeared on behalf of her son. She made a long statement to the Judge concerning her son's circum- stances, and alleged that her son did not know what he was signing when he signed the agreement.—Mr. White stated that the agreement was made out at the defend- ant's own suggestion.—His Honour stid that there was no question that the plaintiff was entitled to possession and he would make an order accordingly. The sum of £1 ss. which was claimed for rent he would reduce to £l,and he would allow £5 14s. for the defendant's breach of contract in not fencing the land. Mrs. Lloyd asked for time to pay the money.—His Honour made an order for £1 per month.

div.head: SCOTCH MINER'S STRIKE.
div.p: THE SCOTCH MINER'S STRIKE.

The Miners' Federation of Great Britain met at Edin- burgh on Thursday to consider the position of the miners' strike in Scotland. Mr. S. Woods, M.P., presided. The meeting was private, but an official report was supplied to the press. From this it appears that Mr. Smillie, presieient of the Scottish Miners' Federatiou, stated that 2.500 men were working on the Federation terms, 500 men were working with the permission of the Federation; and 10.000 men were working on the employers' terms, leaving 55,000 men still in the Cell. They believed it to be possible to bring out again the 10,000 men who had gone ba Ik to work. Reports were presented by the English delegates as to the position of their districts, the financial support rendered during the strike, and the probable amount of assistance which could be given in the event of the continuance af the struggle. The Con- ference then adjourned, on the understanding that the Scottish delegates Should meet to draft a resolution to be submitted to the Conference on Friday. The Scottish delegates then held a brief sitting, at which they re- affirmed their desire for the continuance of the strike and that every effort should be made to bring out on strike again those men who have returned to work. This resolution will be submitted to the Conference to- day, and the Miners' Federation will be asked tosupport it. The continuance of the strike is believed to be practically assured.
LYMM.

PICNIC ox Tan SKIP CANAL.—About 300 tradespeople from Lymm and district joined the steamer "Daniel Adamson " for Liverpool and New Brighton on Monday, their dPstination being reached at a quarter to twelve. The amusements to be obtained in New Brighton were gr, atly enjoyed. The return journey was commenced about 4.30 in the afternoon. On the way home a con- cert was held in the saloon of the steamer, songs being contributed by Messrs. Alexander, T. Peters and Wright. Mr. Barff, in a short speech, spoke of the enjoymentthey had experienced during the day's outing, and congratu- lated Mr. Fairclough and Mr. Rouse on the excellent arraneements they had made. The party reached Lymm about eight o'clock. The day was fine through- out.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

HARVEST FESTIVAL.-1n connection with the Frodsham Parish Church harvest thanksgiving services were cele- brated on Thursday evening and Sunday evening. The Rev. F. W. Willis. M.A.. of Warrington, preached on Thursday, and the Rev.H. B. Blogg, vicar of Frodsham, on Sunday. The decorations were very tasteful,and the offerings abundant. COMPLETION OF THE WATER WORKS.—The work of supplyiug the district of Frodsham was completed on the Bth inst. when the 31 miles of mains were charged with water, along with the service connections to the houses. The pumping station is about 300 yards east of the Gas Works ; and here there is a well and borehole of 300 teet, and "first class " water is forced into a covered reservoir 230 feet above ordnance vatum. The reservoir's c,pacity is 125.000 gallons, and gives ample pressure for fire and domestic requirements. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT KINGSWOOD.—Harvest thanks- giving services were held on Seedily, in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Kingswood. Mr. Shaw, of Manchester, preached in the afternoon and evening. There were excellent congregations, and the collections on the Sun- day amounted to £B. On Monday evening a goodly number of people assembled to hear Mr. Plevison, of M inchester, preach and relate some of his experiences in the Holy Land. The chapel was packed with people and the sermon was highly appreciated. The proceeds of Monday evening's service, and sale, brought the total income of the Harvest Thanksgiving Services up to £l2. The whole effort has succeeded beyond the meat saeguine exneetations. Much praise is due to the efforts of friends for the chapel being so prettily decorated.

RENEWAL OF THE WEAVER TAVERN LICENSE.—At the Oakmere adjourned Licensing Sessions held on Monday at Oakmere, the license of the Weaver Tavern, Prods ham, held by Joseph Faulkner, was ohj.nted to on the ground principally that he was on the 29'h November convicted at Frodsham Petty. Sessions of permitting drunkenness and fined 40s. and costs. Mr. Cartwright, of Chester, appeared on behalf of the applicant, and Mr. J. H. Cooke, of Winsford, opposed the license on behalf of the police. P.C. Wetherly stated that on the lath Octoher.lB93, he visited the Weaver Tavern at nine p.m. Fle found a man there named Stephen Oakes. He was in the taproom very drunk, and leaning upon a table. Beside him was a pint jug half full of beer. Sergeant Thomas drew the landlord's attention to him, and or- dered him home. They followed him, and he fell down. The landlord asked Sergeant Thomas to look over it that time. He admitted that the man was drunk. The land- lord was fined 40s. In answer to the Chairman, Mr Cooke said they did not allege anything against the house. P.C.Price stated that he had been in the district some time. The house had been very well conducted since the conviction took place.—The Chairman said the Bench thought it was quite right that this case should be raised,anci they would like it to be known that they had taken notice of it. They did not think it was a case for the refnsal of the renewal, and considering the appli- cant's good character during the lase ten months, they would rant the renewal of the license.

LECTURE ON " PARISR COUNCILS." —On Wednesday evening a goodly number of people assembled in the Primitive Methodist Chapel to hear a lecture on the above subject by the Rev. H. R. Did cock. Mr. J. M. Williams occupied the chair, and in introducing the lecturer said how important it was that people should make them- selves acquainted with the Parish Councils' Act, and pointed out the beneficial effect which it is calculated to have on village government in the future. Mr. Didcock was then called upon to deliver his lecture. He drew a vivid picture of the present condition of village life in many parts of this country, and pointed out in a very clear manner the provisions of the Act respecting the establiihment of parish meetings in every parish and of oriel) councils in every parish with a population of over 300. The separate powers of parish meetings in parishes where no cmuncil is established were lucidly explained ; the persona of the parish council were dealt with at some length, and special attention was devoted to allotments, purchase of land, charities,and the position and power of women as electors and councillors. The lecturer also gave a brief exposition of the election,povvers and duties of District Councils, closing the lecture by passing in re- view the many important provi Mons which had been elucidated, and drawing a happy picture of the future of the agricultural villages if the electors rose to the height of their opportunity and elected the beet men as councillors. Opport unity was given for questions to be asked of the lecturer upon any point of the new Act. A number of questions were asked by different persons in the audience and were replied to in a very satisfactory manner. On the whole the lecture and discussion were: very instructive. There is room for much more interest to be excited on this subject in Frodsham as many of the people seem very unconcerned as to the powers and duties which this new Act confers upon them. A hearty vote of thanks to the chairman and lecturer brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: MR, GLADSTONiS HEALTH AND
div.p: MR, GLADSTONiS HEALTH AND
SIGHT.

We are glad to be able to state that the operation for cataract performed on Mr. Gladstone's right eye last May has given an excellent result. At the time of our last annotation (issue of July 28) there was enough of residual opacity in the pupil to prevent accurate vision, and it was believed that a needle operation would be required. Subsequently, however, the sight cleared so much that for some weeks past Mr. Gladstone has de- pended entirely upon this eye for reading; so that when, 1(on September 20th) Mr. Nettleship found that the oper- ate,i eye could read the finest print (No. 1 Jager), and see ' distinct objects well, he decided not to interfere. The cataract in the left eye, though still immature, has made progress since the right was operated upon, and this eye is no longer useful for reading ordinary type. Mr. Gladstone is in very good health and spirits, gets through a large amount of reading and writing, and tklv.s walking and carriage exercise daily.—British Medical Journal.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN ON MR, GLADSTONE'S LETTER.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN ON MR, GLAD- STONE'S LETTER.

AN IMPORTANT PRONOUNCEMENT. Mr. Chamberlain was interviewed at his residence ou Wednesday evening by a representative of the Birming- ham "Daily Mail" on the effect that Mr. Gladstone's letter approving of the Gothenburg system was likely to have on the Gladstonian party, and the change it was likely to bring about in temperance legislation. Mr. Chamberlain said that Mr. Gladstone's preference for the Gothenburg system was not a revelation to him. Since he (Mr. Chamberlain) first advocated the reform Mr. Gladstone had otten spoken to him on the subject, and referred to the system in favourable terms. Now the system was coming forward again as an alternative to the unpracticable probibition programme of the local vetoists, and Mr. Gladstone rideased from the trammels
of party in his retirement found himself free to pro- nounce in its favour. Mr. Gladstone had never made a _ _

definite pronouncement in favour of local veto. The most he did was to permit it to be included in the Government programme. Sir William Harcourt was pledged to it no doubt. Mr. Gladstone's declaration would, he thought, set free very many members who were only brought to favour the bill by the pressure of circumstances. If Sir William Harcourt refused to recognise this and brought forward the local veto bill next session he would split the party. That was Mr. Chamberlain's firm opinion. Mr. Chamberlain then proceeded to advocate an experimental trial of the system. If, he said, a town e)f , about 40,000 people would try the experiment, he believed a private bill sanctioning it could be passe-I. Mr. Gladstone's letter had given the movement such a great forward impulse that Parliament might be per- suaded to pass such a bill. The money to buy out the publicans should be raised out of the rates. A Gother- burg scheme bill would give the local authorities compul- sory powers of purchase. Mr. Chamberlain saw nothing in the tied house that would c3inplicate compensation. He rejoiced that Mr. Gladstone had come forward to help the project with the weight of his mature wisdom. In concluding the interview Mr. Chamberlain took occasion to make a very feeling personal allusion to Mr. Gladstone. He confessed himself very much gratifiect by the way in which Mr. Gladstone had expressed his pleasure at Mr. Chamberlain's connection with this. movement. In the outside world some would have it that they were anything but friends since the political party tie that held them so long in common had been severed. He was glad to say, however, that this was very far from the truth. Amidst all the turmoil of poli- tical strife their personal relationship had continued undiminished and unbroken He had received many cherished proofs from Mr. Gladstone of his continued esteem. It was hut very lately that he had visited and he had found the magnanimity and charm of his char- acter and grand personality enhanced, if possible, in his retirment.

div.head: TREASURE TROVE RING. :1
div.p: A TREASURE TROVE RING. :1

While digging ballast in a plot of land in Daubeney- road, Hackney, recently, a labourer struck a bright- looking object with his pick. On examination this proved to be an old-fashioned gold ring, engraved with Latin inscriptions inside, and with figures on the out- side. Mr. Reed, the assistant curator of the British Museum, has expressed the opinion that it was probably one of the sixteen rings which Sir Edward Shaw, Gold- smith and Alderman of the City of London, directed in his will in 1487 to be made as amulets or charms against disease—chiefly cramp—as it is similar in almost every respect to a much larger one in the possession of the authorities which was discovered at CoventrY In 1802. The figures on the outside of the ring represent The Crucifixion, the Virgin and Child, and the third figure might be intended for St. John.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be holden at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 15th day of October next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow. Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming :he Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 15th day of October, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester,. on THURSDAY, the 18th day of October next, at eleven' o'clock in the Forenooß, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY, the 18th day of October next, at eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, 24th September, 1894.
